wrongOptionNotes.A: localStorage is accessible via JavaScript, making tokens stored there highly vulnerable to theft if an XSS vulnerability exists.
wrongOptionNotes.C: sessionStorage is equally accessible via JavaScript as localStorage, leaving tokens vulnerable to XSS.
wrongOptionNotes.D: JavaScript variables are accessible to any script running on the page, leaving them exposed to XSS data exfiltration.

questions.question: An application hosted on AWS Elastic Beanstalk needs to access AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. The developer wants to ensure that the EC2 instances in the Beanstalk environment have the minimum necessary permissions. How should the developer configure these permissions?

options.text: Disable all IAM security controls on the Elastic Beanstalk environment to allow public parameter access.
Attach an inline administrator policy to the default AWS root account.
Modify the Elastic Beanstalk instance profile role to include policies granting read access to specific Parameter Store paths.
Embed AWS administrator credentials in the Elastic Beanstalk software configuration environment properties.

questions.explanation: AWS Elastic Beanstalk provisions an instance profile role for the EC2 instances in the environment. To allow applications running on these instances to interact with AWS services like Systems Manager Parameter Store securely, developers must attach the required permissions directly to this instance profile role.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Disabling IAM security controls compromises the entire application infrastructure.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Using root account credentials or overly broad permissions violates security best practices.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Storing administrator credentials in environment properties exposes highly privileged credentials unnecessarily.

questions.question: A developer is writing code for an AWS Lambda function that will interact with AWS IAM to create temporary user credentials. Which AWS SDK method or best practice should be applied when handling IAM interactions?

options.text: Use the IAM `CreateAccessKey` API on every function invocation to generate permanent access keys.
Hardcode AWS root account keys into the Lambda function deployment package.
Store AWS account master passwords in plain text within environment variables.
Use the AWS Security Token Service (STS) `AssumeRole` API to generate temporary, least-privilege security credentials.

questions.explanation: When applications need temporary access or need to delegate permissions, they should use AWS STS (Security Token Service) APIs such as `AssumeRole` rather than creating permanent IAM access keys. STS issues short-lived credentials that automatically expire.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Creating permanent access keys programmatically on every invocation rapidly exhausts the IAM per-user access key quota and creates severe security risks.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Hardcoding root account keys is a critical security vulnerability.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Storing master passwords in environment variables exposes sensitive credentials.

questions.question: An enterprise application stores credit card data in an Amazon DynamoDB table. Compliance regulations require that all data written to the table is automatically encrypted at rest using an encryption key managed and rotated automatically by AWS, without requiring application-level code changes. Which configuration satisfies this requirement?

options.text: Store the credit card data in plain text and rely on VPC flow logs for encryption.
Enable DynamoDB encryption at rest using an AWS managed KMS key.
Enable DynamoDB encryption at rest using the default AWS owned key.
Write custom encryption logic in the application code using a local AES library before sending data to DynamoDB.

questions.explanation: Amazon DynamoDB provides native encryption at rest using AWS KMS keys. By enabling server-side encryption with an AWS managed key or customer-managed KMS key, DynamoDB encrypts data as it is written to storage and decrypts it when read, entirely transparent to the application code.

wrongOptionNotes.A: VPC flow logs record IP traffic metadata and do not provide data-at-rest encryption.
wrongOptionNotes.C: While AWS owned keys encrypt data, compliance frameworks typically require customer-managed keys (CMKs) or AWS managed keys with distinct auditing and rotation control.
wrongOptionNotes.D: The requirement specifies no application-level code changes; client-side encryption requires custom application logic.

questions.question: A developer is configuring cross-account access for an Amazon S3 bucket located in Account A. An application running in Account B needs to read objects from this bucket. What combination of permissions is required to successfully allow this cross-account access?

options.text: Only an IAM policy attached to the IAM user or role in Account B granting `s3:GetObject` on the bucket ARN.
Public read access enabled on the S3 bucket in Account A.
A bucket policy in Account A granting access to Account B's role, and an IAM policy in Account B granting `s3:GetObject` to the application role.
An AWS Shield policy attached to the S3 bucket in Account A.

questions.explanation: Cross-account access in AWS requires a trust relationship established on both sides. The resource owner must grant explicit access via a resource-based policy (such as an S3 bucket policy), and the principal's administrator in the trusting account must grant permission using an identity-based policy (IAM policy).

wrongOptionNotes.A: Without a corresponding bucket policy in Account A permitting access, IAM policies in Account B alone are insufficient for cross-account access.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Making the bucket public bypasses granular cross-account access controls and violates security best practices.
wrongOptionNotes.D: AWS Shield provides DDoS mitigation, not cross-account authorization.

questions.question: A developer is configuring an AWS Lambda function to process payment transactions. The function requires access to a secret API key stored in AWS Secrets Manager. Which approach adheres to the AWS security best practices for credential management?

options.text: Hardcode the API key inside the Lambda deployment package source code so it is strictly bound to the function revision.
Embed the API key directly in the Lambda environment variables using plaintext string values.
Grant the Lambda execution role permissions to call secretsmanager:GetSecretValue and retrieve the secret programmatically at runtime.
Store the API key in a public Amazon S3 bucket and fetch it using an unauthenticated HTTP GET request.

questions.explanation: AWS Secrets Manager securely stores and rotates credentials. Applications should use IAM execution roles to grant least-privilege access, retrieving secrets programmatically at runtime to avoid hardcoding or static environment variable exposure.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Hardcoding secrets in source code violates security best practices and exposes credentials in version control systems.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Environment variables are visible in the console and via API descriptions, making plaintext secrets vulnerable to accidental exposure.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Storing secrets in a public S3 bucket exposes sensitive data to the entire internet.

questions.question: A developer needs to configure AWS IAM policies for a backend microservice running on Amazon ECS. The service only needs to read items from a specific Amazon DynamoDB table named Orders. Which IAM policy follows the principle of least privilege?

options.text: Allow actions dynamodb:GetItem and dynamodb:Query specifically restricted to the Amazon Resource Name (ARN) of the Orders table.
Allow all dynamodb:* actions scoped to the Amazon Resource Name (ARN) of the Orders table.
Allow all actions on all resources '*' in the AWS account to ensure no permission errors occur.
Allow dynamodb:GetItem on all DynamoDB tables across the entire AWS region.

questions.explanation: The principle of least privilege dictates granting only the specific permissions needed to perform a task. For DynamoDB access, this means specifying exact actions (like GetItem) and scoping resources to specific table ARNs.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Allowing all DynamoDB actions grants write and administrative privileges when only read access is required.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Granting wildcards for all actions and resources violates the principle of least privilege and significantly expands the blast radius.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Scoping the permission to all tables in the region is overly broad when access is only required for a single table.

questions.question: An application hosted on an Amazon EC2 instance needs to securely generate digital signatures using a master key without exposing the key material outside of a secure hardware module. Which AWS service should the developer integrate with?

options.text: AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store Standard tier
Amazon S3 bucket policy encryption
Amazon Cognito User Pools cryptographic module
AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS)

questions.explanation: AWS KMS is integrated with AWS CloudHSM and provides centralized control over cryptographic keys. It allows applications to call APIs like Sign and Verify without exposing the underlying key material.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Parameter Store stores configuration data and secrets, but does not provide cryptographic operations like digital signatures backed by HSMs.
wrongOptionNotes.B: S3 bucket policies control access to S3 objects, not application-level cryptographic signing operations.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Amazon Cognito manages user identities and authentication tokens, not arbitrary application cryptographic signing.

questions.question: A developer is building a public web API using Amazon API Gateway and AWS Lambda. To protect against unauthorized access, the developer wants to authenticate clients using JSON Web Tokens (JWT) issued by a third-party identity provider. What is the most efficient way to implement this?

options.text: Write a custom AWS Lambda function to inspect incoming HTTP headers, decode the JWT, verify its cryptographic signature manually, and cache the public keys.
Store all user passwords in an Amazon DynamoDB table and have the API Gateway route queries directly to validate credentials on every request.
Configure an Amazon Cognito user pool authorizer or a JWT authorizer directly on the API Gateway routes.
Attach an IAM resource policy to the API Gateway endpoint requiring SigV4 signing for all public internet requests.

questions.explanation: API Gateway native JWT authorizers offload token validation (checking expiration, issuer, audience, and cryptographic signatures) directly to the API Gateway edge, reducing latency and operational overhead.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Writing custom validation logic in a Lambda authorizer is inefficient when API Gateway offers native JWT authorizers that handle signature verification automatically.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Validating passwords directly on every request is a severe security risk and undermines token-based authentication standards.
wrongOptionNotes.D: SigV4 signing is designed for AWS internal services and developer integrations, not public-facing web clients using third-party identity providers.

questions.question: A developer needs to ensure that all objects uploaded to an Amazon S3 bucket are encrypted at rest using a customer-managed key stored in AWS KMS. Which configuration should be applied to the S3 bucket?

options.text: Rely solely on client-side encryption without configuring any bucket-level settings.
Enable default encryption on the S3 bucket specifying AWS KMS (SSE-KMS) with a customer-managed KMS key.
Attach an IAM user policy to every developer allowing PutObject actions.
Enable Amazon S3 Versioning and lifecycle rules.

questions.explanation: S3 default encryption with SSE-KMS enforces server-side encryption for all incoming objects, ensuring compliance with organizational security mandates regarding customer-managed keys.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Relying on client-side encryption leaves the bucket unprotected if a client accidentally uploads unencrypted objects.
wrongOptionNotes.C: IAM policies manage permissions to perform actions, but do not enforce server-side encryption settings on bucket objects.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Versioning and lifecycle rules manage object history and storage tiers, not encryption enforcement.

questions.question: A web application hosted on Amazon EC2 needs to authenticate users and manage sessions securely. The development team wants to avoid building custom user management, password hashing, and multi-factor authentication. Which AWS service should they integrate?

options.text: AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM)
AWS Shield
AWS Systems Manager
Amazon Cognito

questions.explanation: Amazon Cognito is a fully managed identity service designed for web and mobile applications, providing secure user directories, authentication, and federation with social or enterprise identity providers.

wrongOptionNotes.A: IAM is designed for managing AWS administrative accounts and programmatic access keys for internal resources, not public web application end-users.
wrongOptionNotes.B: AWS Shield is a managed DDoS protection service, not an identity provider or user directory.
wrongOptionNotes.C: AWS Systems Manager is used for operational insights and instance management, not end-user authentication.

questions.question: An enterprise application requires that database credentials stored in AWS Secrets Manager are automatically rotated every 30 days without application downtime. How should the developer configure this?

options.text: Use AWS IAM credential report generation to trigger password resets.
Write a cron job on an Amazon EC2 instance to overwrite the secret value manually every month.
Configure automatic rotation in Secrets Manager using an AWS Lambda rotation function that updates both the database and the secret.
Set an Amazon S3 lifecycle policy to delete and recreate the secret every 30 days.

questions.explanation: AWS Secrets Manager integrates with AWS Lambda to automate secret rotation. The Lambda function handles changing the password in the database, updating the secret, and testing the new credentials.

wrongOptionNotes.A: IAM credential reports are for auditing, not automated database credential rotation.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Manual cron jobs are prone to failure, lack built-in retry mechanisms, and do not handle the complex multi-step rotation lifecycle safely.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Secrets Manager secrets cannot be managed or rotated via S3 lifecycle policies.

questions.question: A developer is writing code that runs on AWS Lambda and needs to assume an IAM role in another AWS account to access a shared Amazon S3 bucket. Which API call should the developer use to obtain temporary security credentials?

options.text: iam:CreateAccessKey to generate permanent programmatic credentials for the target account
s3:GetBucketLocation using the Amazon S3 client
secretsmanager:GetSecretValue to retrieve root account credentials
sts:AssumeRole using the AWS Security Token Service (STS) client

questions.explanation: AWS STS AssumeRole allows an IAM role in one account to request temporary, limited-privilege credentials to access resources in another account when trusted by a cross-account IAM policy.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Creating permanent access keys for cross-account access violates security best practices and introduces severe credential leakage risks.
wrongOptionNotes.B: GetBucketLocation only returns the geographic region of an S3 bucket, it does not handle cross-account authentication.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Root account credentials should never be retrieved or used by application code.

questions.question: A company requires that all source code repositories and build artifacts stored in Amazon S3 must be encrypted using keys that the security team can independently disable and audit at any time. Which encryption method meets this requirement?

options.text: Client-side hashing with MD5 checksums
Unencrypted storage with HTTPS transport-layer encryption only
AWS KMS Customer Managed Keys (CMKs)
Amazon S3 Managed Keys (SSE-S3)

questions.explanation: AWS KMS Customer Managed Keys (CMKs) provide granular access control, audit trails through AWS CloudTrail, and the ability to instantly revoke access by disabling the key.

wrongOptionNotes.A: MD5 checksums verify data integrity, not encryption.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Transport encryption (TLS) protects data in transit, but leaves data unencrypted at rest in the storage medium.
wrongOptionNotes.D: SSE-S3 keys are fully managed by AWS behind the scenes, offering no customer visibility, manual key rotation control, or granular disable capabilities.

questions.question: A developer is configuring an Amazon API Gateway REST API and needs to restrict incoming requests to only those originating from a specific corporate network IP address range. How can this be implemented?

options.text: Configure an Amazon S3 bucket policy with IP address restrictions.
Set the API endpoint type to Edge-optimized and modify the AWS Route 53 DNS resolver settings.
Write a custom AWS IAM policy attached to the API Gateway stage variables.
Attach an AWS WAF Web ACL containing IP match conditions to the API Gateway stage.

questions.explanation: AWS WAF integrates directly with Amazon API Gateway, allowing developers to define Web ACLs with IP sets to whitelist or blacklist specific client IP ranges.

wrongOptionNotes.A: S3 bucket policies control access to S3 objects, not API Gateway HTTP endpoints.
wrongOptionNotes.B: DNS resolvers route traffic based on domain names, not HTTP client IP filtering.
wrongOptionNotes.C: API Gateway stage variables do not evaluate IP address conditions; IAM resource policies or WAF are required.

questions.question: An application running on AWS Lambda needs to decrypt configuration data that was encrypted using an AWS KMS customer-managed key. What permission must be included in the Lambda execution role?

options.text: ec2:DescribeInstances permission for network discovery
s3:GetObject permission on the Lambda deployment package bucket
dynamodb:PutItem permission on the configuration table
kms:Decrypt permission scoped to the specific KMS key ARN

questions.explanation: AWS KMS requires both IAM policies (granting the principal kms:Decrypt permission) and KMS key policies (allowing the principal to use the key) to successfully perform cryptographic operations.

wrongOptionNotes.A: EC2 permissions relate to virtual servers and networking, not KMS key decryption.
wrongOptionNotes.B: S3 permissions grant access to retrieve objects from storage buckets, not to perform KMS cryptographic decryption operations.
wrongOptionNotes.C: DynamoDB permissions manage database table records, not KMS key cryptographic operations.

questions.question: A developer is implementing token-based authentication for a mobile app using Amazon Cognito User Pools. After a user successfully signs in, the application receives an ID token, an access token, and a refresh token. Which token should the application use to authorize API requests to backend APIs protected by an API Gateway authorizer?

options.text: The access token
The refresh token
The ID token
The AWS root account secret access key

questions.explanation: In OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect frameworks implemented by Amazon Cognito, access tokens carry authorization scopes and are sent to backend APIs, whereas ID tokens carry identity claims for the user interface.

wrongOptionNotes.B: The refresh token is used exclusively with the Cognito token endpoint to obtain new access and ID tokens when they expire.
wrongOptionNotes.C: The ID token contains user identity claims (like email and username) meant for UI display, not API authorization.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Root credentials should never be embedded in mobile or client-side applications.

questions.question: A developer needs to store database connection strings securely in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. The values must be encrypted at rest and accessible only by authorized applications. Which parameter type is appropriate?

options.text: SecureString
Binary
String
StringList

questions.explanation: Systems Manager Parameter Store supports SecureString parameters, which automatically encrypt sensitive data at rest using either default AWS managed keys or customer-managed KMS keys.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Binary parameters store binary payloads and are not designed for encrypted textual configuration secrets.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Standard string parameters are stored in plaintext and do not provide encryption at rest.
wrongOptionNotes.D: StringList parameters store comma-separated values in plaintext without encryption.

questions.question: An enterprise application stores personally identifiable information (PII) in an Amazon DynamoDB table. Compliance mandates that all table data must be encrypted at rest using an encryption key managed entirely by the organization in AWS KMS. How should the developer configure this?

options.text: Enable DynamoDB table encryption using a Customer Managed Key (CMK) from AWS KMS.
Rely on DynamoDB default AWS owned keys.
Encrypt every attribute value in application code using custom keys before writing to DynamoDB.
Attach an IAM permissions boundary to all database users.

questions.explanation: DynamoDB server-side encryption allows customers to protect table data at rest using AWS KMS Customer Managed Keys, providing full control and compliance alignment.

wrongOptionNotes.B: AWS owned keys are managed by DynamoDB service accounts and do not give the customer direct control, rotation oversight, or auditing capabilities required by strict compliance mandates.
wrongOptionNotes.C: While client-side encryption is valid, native DynamoDB server-side encryption with CMKs provides transparent encryption without adding application-layer processing overhead.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Permissions boundaries restrict maximum permissions, but do not encrypt data at rest.

questions.question: A developer is configuring cross-account access for an Amazon S3 bucket. Account A owns the S3 bucket, and an application running in Account B needs to read objects from it. What combination of configurations is required to allow this access?

options.text: Account A must configure an S3 bucket policy granting access to Account B, and Account B must grant its application IAM role permissions to access the bucket.
Only Account B needs to create an S3 bucket policy.
Only Account A needs to create an IAM user with administrative access.
Configure public read access on the S3 bucket in Account A.

questions.explanation: Cross-account access requires a trust relationship established by both the resource policy (S3 bucket policy in Account A) and the identity-based policy (IAM policy in Account B).

wrongOptionNotes.B: Account B cannot apply policies to a bucket it does not own in Account A.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Sharing administrative users across accounts violates security best practices and does not establish proper resource trust.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Making an S3 bucket public violates security policies and exposes sensitive data to the entire internet.

questions.question: A developer is building a serverless data ingestion pipeline where a Python application running on AWS Lambda needs to retrieve API keys and database connection strings dynamically at runtime. The security team mandates that these sensitive secrets must be rotated automatically on a regular schedule without modifying application code, and the access to the secrets must be audited via AWS CloudTrail. Which storage solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Store the secrets in AWS Secrets Manager and configure native automatic rotation using an AWS Lambda rotation function.
Store the secrets in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store as SecureString parameters and use Amazon EventBridge to trigger a manual update script every 30 days.
Embed the encrypted credentials directly within the AWS Lambda environment variables using AWS KMS customer managed keys.
Store the credentials in an encrypted JSON file inside an Amazon S3 bucket, and use S3 Versioning to track changes.

questions.explanation: AWS Secrets Manager is designed specifically for managing and automatically rotating credentials, API keys, and database passwords. It integrates natively with AWS Lambda to execute rotation logic and logs all retrieval actions to AWS CloudTrail.

wrongOptionNotes.B: While Parameter Store supports SecureString, it lacks native automated secret rotation integration with AWS Lambda compared to Secrets Manager, requiring custom scripting and maintenance.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Environment variables do not support automated rotation without redeploying the Lambda function, making this approach impractical for frequent secret updates.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Storing production credentials in an S3 file does not provide native automatic rotation capabilities or fine-grained secret management features.

questions.question: An application running on an Amazon EC2 instance needs to securely upload sensitive medical documents to an Amazon S3 bucket. Compliance regulations require that the objects must be encrypted at rest on the server side using a unique encryption key that is managed entirely by the developer, and the key material must never be stored or persisted by AWS. Which encryption mechanism should the developer implement?

options.text: Client-Side Encryption with an AWS KMS customer managed key
Server-Side Encryption with Customer-Provided Keys (SSE-C)
Server-Side Encryption with Amazon S3 Managed Keys (SSE-S3)
Server-Side Encryption with AWS KMS Keys (SSE-KMS)

questions.explanation: Server-Side Encryption with Customer-Provided Keys (SSE-C) enables you to set your own encryption keys. Amazon S3 performs the encryption on write and decryption on read, but it immediately discards the encryption key and does not store it.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Client-side encryption encrypts the data on the EC2 instance before sending it, but it typically relies on AWS KMS to store or manage keys, failing the constraint that key material must never be persisted by AWS.
wrongOptionNotes.C: SSE-S3 uses keys managed completely by AWS, which does not satisfy the requirement for the developer to manage the key material.
wrongOptionNotes.D: SSE-KMS utilizes keys stored and managed within AWS KMS, whereas the requirement dictates that key material must be provided and managed externally without AWS storing it.

questions.question: A developer is configuring an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of an Application Load Balancer. To ensure that users cannot bypass CloudFront and access the backend load balancer directly, the developer wants to restrict traffic so that the ALB only accepts requests originating from the specific CloudFront distribution. Which configuration approach should the developer use?

options.text: Configure a custom header in CloudFront to the origin request and use AWS WAF on the ALB to verify the secret header value.
Implement AWS WAF on the Application Load Balancer and create a rule to inspect and block requests lacking a custom user-agent string.
Update the Amazon EC2 security groups attached to the ALB to allow inbound traffic only from the public IP addresses of the client.
Configure an origin access control (OAC) on CloudFront and add a header check condition on the ALB listener rules.

questions.explanation: To secure an ALB origin behind CloudFront, developers typically configure CloudFront to send a custom header (e.g., X-Custom-Header) with a secret value. The ALB or an attached AWS WAF web ACL is then configured to inspect incoming requests and drop any traffic that does not include this valid secret header.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Custom user-agent strings can be easily spoofed by malicious clients bypassing CloudFront, making this an insecure method for access restriction.
wrongOptionNotes.C: CloudFront's edge node IP addresses change dynamically and are shared globally, making static security group IP rules unfeasible and insecure.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Origin Access Control (OAC) is specifically designed for Amazon S3 origins, not for Application Load Balancers.

questions.question: A development team has deployed a web application on Amazon EC2 instances that interact with various AWS services, including Amazon DynamoDB and Amazon S3. During a security review, it is discovered that long-lived IAM user access keys were hardcoded into the application configuration files on the EC2 instances. What is the most secure and recommended practice to remediate this vulnerability?

options.text: Rotate the hardcoded IAM user access keys every 30 days using an automated script and restrict the IAM policy to specific source IP ranges.
Delete the hardcoded IAM user access keys, create an IAM role with the required permissions, and attach the role directly to the Amazon EC2 instance profile.
Encrypt the configuration file containing the access keys using an AWS KMS key and decrypt it in memory during the application boot phase.
Remove the hardcoded keys and store them securely in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store as encrypted SecureString parameters retrieved at application startup.

questions.explanation: Applications running on Amazon EC2 should never use long-lived IAM user credentials. Instead, you should assign an IAM role to an EC2 instance profile. AWS automatically provides temporary security credentials to the instance, which the AWS SDKs use transparently.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Rotating static access keys does not solve the underlying risk of credential exposure and operational overhead associated with managing long-lived keys.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Encrypting static keys still relies on IAM user access keys, which violates AWS security best practices for compute resources.
wrongOptionNotes.D: While Parameter Store securely stores parameters, using IAM user access keys remains an anti-pattern when running code on EC2. Instance roles are the native, preferred approach.

questions.question: A developer is configuring an AWS CodePipeline pipeline that deploys a serverless application using AWS SAM. The pipeline contains a source stage and a build stage. The developer needs to ensure that the CloudFormation stack is automatically updated whenever changes are pushed to the GitHub repository without requiring manual approval steps. Which action should be added to the buildspec.yml file to accomplish this?

options.text: Use the sam package command followed by the sam deploy command with the --no-confirm-changeset and --no-fail-on-empty-changeset flags.
Use the aws cloudformation create-stack command to deploy the generated template directly.
Use the sam package command and upload the artifact to an Amazon S3 bucket without invoking sam deploy.
Add an AWS::CodePipeline::Approval action block inside the buildspec.yml file.

questions.explanation: AWS SAM utilizes the AWS CLI and AWS CloudFormation under the hood. To automate deployments in CI/CD pipelines like AWS CodePipeline without manual intervention, developers use 'sam deploy --no-confirm-changeset --no-fail-on-empty-changeset', which bypasses interactive prompts and handles empty change sets gracefully.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Using create-stack will fail on subsequent pipeline executions because the stack already exists. The update-stack command or sam deploy should be used instead.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Merely packaging the application and uploading it to S3 only prepares the artifact; it does not deploy or update the CloudFormation stack or serverless resources.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Manual approval actions are configured within the pipeline definition in AWS CloudFormation or the CodePipeline console, not inside a buildspec.yml file.

questions.question: An enterprise developer is managing a Node.js web application deployed on AWS Elastic Beanstalk. The application experiences frequent traffic spikes during business hours. During these spikes, the underlying Amazon EC2 instances become overloaded before auto scaling policies can react, resulting in downtime. The developer needs to implement a deployment strategy that minimizes disruption and allows fast rollbacks while maintaining application availability. Which configuration is most appropriate?

options.text: Configure Elastic Beanstalk to use the Immutable deployment policy.
Configure Elastic Beanstalk to use the Rolling deployment policy with a batch size of 100%.
Configure Elastic Beanstalk to use the Rolling with Additional Batch deployment policy.
Configure Elastic Beanstalk to use the AllAtOnce deployment policy.

questions.explanation: Elastic Beanstalk offers multiple deployment policies. Immutable deployment ensures that an entire set of replacement instances is fully provisioned and validated before any traffic is shifted to them. If a deployment fails, traffic remains untouched on the old instances, and the new stack can be discarded immediately.

wrongOptionNotes.B: A batch size of 100% behaves similarly to an AllAtOnce deployment, taking instances out of service simultaneously and risking application availability.
wrongOptionNotes.C: While this policy launches an extra batch of instances to maintain capacity, it still updates existing instances in place and is slower and less robust for zero-downtime rollbacks compared to Immutable deployments.
wrongOptionNotes.D: AllAtOnce deploys the new version to all running instances simultaneously, causing downtime and increasing the risk of overloads during traffic spikes.

questions.question: A developer has written a Python script to automate database schema migrations as part of an AWS CodeBuild project. The script needs to connect to an Amazon RDS MySQL database located in a private subnet within a VPC. The CodeBuild project is currently configured with default settings, and the build fails due to a connection timeout when trying to reach the database endpoint. What must the developer do to allow CodeBuild to connect to the RDS instance?

options.text: Create an Amazon API Gateway endpoint in front of the RDS database to proxy migration requests from CodeBuild.
Deploy a NAT gateway in the public subnet and route all CodeBuild traffic through it.
Modify the Amazon RDS security group to allow inbound traffic from the public IP address range of the CodeBuild service.
Configure the CodeBuild project to run within the same VPC, assign private subnets, and associate a security group that allows outbound access to the RDS security group.

questions.explanation: When an AWS CodeBuild build needs to interact with resources in a private VPC (such as an RDS database, ElastiCache cluster, or internal ALB), the CodeBuild project must be configured with VPC settings. This includes providing the VPC ID, private subnet IDs, and a security group that has network access to the target resource.

wrongOptionNotes.A: API Gateway cannot natively proxy direct database protocols like MySQL, making this an overly complex and insecure architectural pattern for database migrations.
wrongOptionNotes.B: A NAT gateway provides outbound access to the public internet, but database traffic destined for a private RDS instance within the same VPC should traverse local VPC routing, not the internet via a NAT gateway.
wrongOptionNotes.C: CodeBuild runs in a managed environment and does not have a static public IP address that can be reliably whitelisted in an RDS security group if it needs to access a private VPC.

questions.question: An application is deployed on Amazon ECS using the AWS Fargate launch type. The development team wants to implement a CI/CD pipeline using AWS CodePipeline and AWS CodeBuild. During the build phase, CodeBuild needs to build a Docker image, tag it, and push it to an Amazon Elastic Container Registry (ECR) repository. Which combination of steps must be included in the buildspec.yml file to successfully authenticate and push the image?

options.text: Store the ECR static username and password in AWS Secrets Manager and reference them directly in the docker login command.
Execute the aws ecs update-service command inside the buildspec to trigger the image build and push process automatically.
Use the aws ecr get-login-password command to log in to Docker, build the image with docker build, tag it, and push it using docker push.
Configure the buildspec to run the ecs-deploy CLI tool, which automatically handles ECR authentication and ECS task updates.

questions.explanation: To push Docker images to Amazon ECR from AWS CodeBuild, the build environment must first authenticate with ECR. This is achieved by running `aws ecr get-login-password --region <region> | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin <account-id>.dkr.ecr.<region>.amazonaws.com`, followed by standard Docker build and push commands.

wrongOptionNotes.A: ECR does not use static IAM usernames and passwords; authentication requires dynamic tokens generated via the `aws ecr get-login-password` command using IAM permissions.
wrongOptionNotes.B: The `aws ecs update-service` command updates an existing service configuration or forces a new deployment; it does not build Docker images or push them to ECR.
wrongOptionNotes.D: While ecs-deploy is a utility script, standard best practices involve using standard AWS CLI and Docker commands within CodeBuild, and ecs-deploy is not a native part of the standard CodeBuild image workflow.

questions.question: A developer is updating an AWS CloudFormation template that provisions an Amazon DynamoDB table and a Lambda function. During a stack update, the developer needs to ensure that the existing DynamoDB table is not accidentally deleted or replaced if a property change forces a physical resource replacement. Which CloudFormation template property should the developer implement?

options.text: Wrap the DynamoDB resource inside a CloudFormation Dynamic Reference block.
Add an UpdatePolicy set to SafeReplace on the DynamoDB table resource.
Enable termination protection on the CloudFormation stack via the AWS CLI.
Add a DeletionPolicy set to Retain on the DynamoDB table resource.

questions.explanation: CloudFormation DeletionPolicy controls how resources are handled when they are removed from a stack or when a stack update forces resource replacement. Setting `DeletionPolicy: Retain` ensures that if a resource like an Amazon S3 bucket or DynamoDB table is replaced due to property changes, the original physical resource and its data are preserved.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Dynamic references are used to safely retrieve values from AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store or Secrets Manager within a template, not to control resource replacement behavior.
wrongOptionNotes.B: UpdatePolicy is used for specific resources like Auto Scaling groups, ElastiCache clusters, and Lambda aliases to manage updates, but it is not a valid attribute to prevent DynamoDB replacement.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Stack termination protection protects the entire CloudFormation stack from being deleted entirely; it does not prevent individual resource replacement during stack updates.

questions.question: A development team uses AWS OpsWorks to manage a fleet of application servers. The lead developer needs to update the application code across all instances in a layer without replacing the instances or causing downtime. Which lifecycle event should the developer trigger to execute the custom deployment recipes?

options.text: Trigger the Setup lifecycle event.
Trigger the Rebuild lifecycle event.
Trigger the Configure lifecycle event.
Trigger the Deploy lifecycle event.

questions.explanation: AWS OpsWorks Stacks uses Chef recipes executed during specific lifecycle events: Setup, Configure, Deploy, Undeploy, and Shutdown. To deploy or update application code on running instances, the Deploy event is invoked.

wrongOptionNotes.A: The Setup lifecycle event runs once when an instance is booted up to install packages and configure the operating system, not for routine application code updates.
wrongOptionNotes.B: OpsWorks does not have a 'Rebuild' lifecycle event; instances are typically updated via standard deployment events or by running instance re-provisioning.
wrongOptionNotes.C: The Configure lifecycle event runs on all instances in the stack whenever an instance comes online or goes offline, updating configuration files, but it is not intended for manual application deployment.

questions.question: An AWS Lambda function is packaged as a container image stored in Amazon ECR. A developer has updated the application code, built a new container image, and pushed it to ECR with the latest tag. However, when invoking the Lambda function, it still executes the older version of the code. What action must the developer take to make Lambda use the new container image?

options.text: Modify the Lambda function timeout setting to force a cache invalidation.
Update the Lambda function configuration to point to the new image digest or publish a new version/update the function code reference.
Delete the old ECR repository and create a new one with the same name.
Restart the Lambda execution role via AWS IAM.

questions.explanation: Lambda functions backed by container images cache the image used during deployment. Simply pushing a new image to ECR with an existing tag does not automatically update the running Lambda function. The function configuration must be updated to pull the latest image digest.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Changing the timeout setting adjusts how long a function can run; it has no effect on container image caching or deployment updates.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Deleting and recreating the repository is disruptive and unnecessary; updating the function configuration is the standard deployment mechanism.
wrongOptionNotes.D: IAM execution roles control permissions, not function code or container image caching.

questions.question: A developer is configuring AWS CodeDeploy to deploy a microservice to an Amazon ECS cluster using an ECS deployment type. The deployment configuration needs to ensure that 10% of the production traffic is shifted to the new task set immediately, and the remaining 90% is shifted after a 5-minute linear baking period. Which deployment configuration should the developer choose?

options.text: CodeDeployDefault.LambdaLinear10PercentEvery10Minutes
CodeDeployDefault.ECSAllAtOnce
CodeDeployDefault.ECSCanary10Percent5Minutes
CodeDeployDefault.ECSLinear10PercentEvery5Minutes

questions.explanation: CodeDeploy provides predefined deployment configurations for ECS and Lambda. Linear configurations (such as CodeDeployDefault.ECSLinear10PercentEvery5Minutes) shift traffic in equal increments at specified intervals, whereas canary configurations shift a percentage, wait, and then move the rest.

wrongOptionNotes.A: This configuration is intended for AWS Lambda deployments, not Amazon ECS container deployments.
wrongOptionNotes.B: This strategy shifts all traffic to the new task set at once, providing no gradual baking or validation period.
wrongOptionNotes.C: A canary deployment shifts a specific percentage (e.g., 10%) of traffic, waits for a specified time (e.g., 5 minutes), and then shifts 100% of the remaining traffic all at once, rather than shifting linearly.

questions.question: A developer has created an AWS CloudFormation template that deploys a complex web application architecture. During testing, a deployment error occurs in a nested stack, causing the entire root stack creation to fail. By default, what action does CloudFormation take when a stack creation fails?

options.text: It automatically escalates the error to AWS Support and creates an incident ticket.
It pauses the stack creation and leaves all provisioned resources running in an UPDATE_COMPLETE_CLEANUP_FAILED state for manual debugging.
It keeps all successfully provisioned resources intact and terminates only the resource that failed.
It automatically rolls back all changes and deletes all successfully created resources within the stack, unless rollback is explicitly disabled.

questions.explanation: CloudFormation rollback on failure is enabled by default. If a stack creation fails, CloudFormation rolls back the stack and deletes all resources created during that execution. Developers can override this behavior using `--disable-rollback` (or equivalent console options) for troubleshooting purposes.

wrongOptionNotes.A: AWS CloudFormation does not automatically create AWS Support tickets upon stack failures.
wrongOptionNotes.B: CloudFormation does not pause by default on failure unless the --disable-rollback flag is explicitly provided during creation.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Keeping provisioned resources on failure only happens if rollback is explicitly disabled when the stack is created.

questions.question: A developer is writing an AWS Lambda function in Python that requires external third-party libraries not included in the standard Python runtime. The deployment package exceeds the inline code editor size limit. What is the most efficient way to package and deploy this Lambda function along with its dependencies?

options.text: Install the dependencies locally into a project directory using pip install -t ., zip the code and dependencies together, and upload the zip file to Lambda or Amazon S3.
Upload the raw python script to Lambda and write a custom bootstrap script to download the dependencies from PyPI during every function invocation.
Store the dependencies in an Amazon EBS volume and attach it to the Lambda execution environment.
Create an Amazon DynamoDB table to store the third-party libraries and import them dynamically at runtime.

questions.explanation: To include external dependencies in an AWS Lambda function, developers typically install dependencies to a local directory using `pip install -r requirements.txt -t .`, bundle the folder into a .zip archive, and deploy it to Lambda (or upload it to S3 for larger archives). Alternatively, Lambda Layers can be used for shared dependencies.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Downloading dependencies from PyPI on every invocation increases latency, violates best practices, and can fail if PyPI experiences an outage or if the execution environment lacks internet access.
wrongOptionNotes.C: AWS Lambda does not support attaching Amazon EBS volumes to function execution environments.
wrongOptionNotes.D: DynamoDB is a NoSQL database and cannot store or execute compiled Python modules or package libraries in a way that Python's import system can resolve.

questions.question: A developer is implementing an AWS CloudFormation template that deploys an application. The template requires different parameter values depending on whether the stack is deployed to a staging environment or a production environment. To maintain clean templates, the developer decides to separate environment-specific parameter configurations. How can this requirement be achieved?

options.text: Store the parameters inside an Amazon RDS database and have CloudFormation query the database during stack creation.
Create separate CloudFormation configuration files (JSON format) containing parameter key-value pairs, and pass the appropriate file using the --parameters flag during deployment.
Hardcode the environment checks inside the CloudFormation template using native Python if-else blocks.
Write a bash script that uses regular expressions to modify the CloudFormation template file in place before every deployment.

questions.explanation: CloudFormation supports passing parameters via external JSON parameter files using the AWS CLI. This practice allows a single template to be reused across multiple environments (staging, production) simply by swapping the parameter configuration file.

wrongOptionNotes.A: CloudFormation cannot query an RDS database directly to resolve stack parameters during the initialization phase.
wrongOptionNotes.C: CloudFormation templates are written in JSON or YAML, not Python, and conditional logic is handled via Mappings or Conditions, not hardcoding.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Modifying templates in place with regex is error-prone and violates infrastructure-as-code best practices, whereas parameter files provide a native, supported mechanism.

questions.question: A development team is using AWS CodeCommit for source control and AWS CodePipeline for CI/CD. The team wants to trigger an automated security scanning tool (AWS Lambda function) whenever a developer pushes a commit to the main branch of the CodeCommit repository. Which service integration should the developer configure to trigger the Lambda function directly?

options.text: Add a webhook definition inside the CodeBuild buildspec.yml file pointing to the CodeCommit repository.
Create an Amazon SNS topic subscription inside the CodeCommit repository settings pointing to the Lambda function endpoint.
Configure an Amazon EventBridge rule that listens for CodeCommit repository state-change events and invokes the Lambda function as a target.
Configure an AWS CloudTrail trail to poll CodeCommit API calls and execute a Lambda function synchronously.

questions.explanation: AWS CodeCommit events (such as branch creation, pushes, or pull request updates) are automatically sent to Amazon EventBridge. Developers can configure EventBridge rules with event patterns targeting CodeCommit to invoke downstream AWS Lambda functions or other targets securely.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Webhooks in CodeBuild are typically used for external repositories like GitHub or Bitbucket, and buildspec files do not manage repository webhook triggers.
wrongOptionNotes.B: While CodeCommit can trigger SNS topics for notifications, EventBridge is the standard and most robust event-driven mechanism for capturing granular repository actions and routing them to Lambda.
wrongOptionNotes.D: CloudTrail logs API activity to S3 or CloudWatch Logs; it does not synchronously trigger Lambda functions based on repository push events.

questions.question: A developer needs to deploy a containerized web application to Amazon ECS using the EC2 launch type. The application requires sensitive database credentials to be securely injected into the container environment at runtime without hardcoding them in the ECS task definition or Dockerfile. What is the most secure and recommended approach?

options.text: Store the credentials in an unencrypted file in an Amazon S3 bucket, and configure the container entrypoint script to download the file on startup.
Encode the database credentials in Base64 and place them directly in the task definition environment variables array.
Store the credentials in AWS Secrets Manager or Systems Manager Parameter Store, and reference them in the task definition under the secrets section so ECS injects them as environment variables.
Mount an Amazon EFS file system containing the cleartext password file into every container instance.

questions.explanation: Amazon ECS allows referencing sensitive data stored in AWS Secrets Manager or AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store directly within container definitions. ECS resolves these references securely when starting the task and injects them into the container environment.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Storing unencrypted credentials in S3 and downloading them via custom scripts introduces significant security risks, including potential exposure in logs or container layers.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Base64 encoding is not encryption. Anyone with read access to the task definition can easily decode the credentials, violating security best practices.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Storing cleartext secrets on a shared EFS volume is insecure and lacks the fine-grained access control and auditing provided by Secrets Manager.

questions.question: An enterprise developer is managing a legacy .NET application deployed on Windows Server instances using AWS Elastic Beanstalk. The application requires frequent configuration changes and custom IIS setup steps during deployments. The developer wants to execute PowerShell scripts automatically during specific phases of the deployment lifecycle. Where should the developer place these scripts?

options.text: Place the scripts in an Amazon S3 bucket and configure an AWS Lambda function to execute them via SSH after deployment.
Embed the PowerShell scripts directly inside the AWS CloudFormation template Outputs section.
Place the PowerShell scripts inside a folder named .ebextensions in the root of the source bundle and configure them using container_commands or files keys.
Package the scripts inside the Amazon RDS database and invoke them using stored procedures.

questions.explanation: Elastic Beanstalk configuration files (`.ebextensions/*.config`) allow developers to customize the environment and configure instances. On Windows platforms, configuration files can execute PowerShell commands and scripts during deployment by using keys such as `commands` or `container_commands`.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Using SSH and Lambda to manually trigger scripts post-deployment is cumbersome, unreliable, and bypasses native Elastic Beanstalk configuration management.
wrongOptionNotes.B: The Outputs section of a CloudFormation template is used to display information about provisioned resources, not to execute operating system commands.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Database stored procedures cannot configure operating system settings or manage IIS server configurations on Windows instances.

questions.question: A developer is configuring an AWS CloudFormation template to deploy an application stack. The template needs to dynamically fetch the latest Amazon Linux 2 AMI ID based on the deployment region without hardcoding the AMI ID in the template. Which CloudFormation feature should the developer use?

options.text: Write a custom AWS Lambda function invoked inside a CloudFormation custom resource to call describe-images on every stack creation.
Use an Amazon S3 bucket to store a global text file containing the latest AMI ID and download it during stack creation.
Use AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store public parameters (Systems Manager Parameter) within the template via dynamic references or AWS-specific parameter types.
Hardcode an extensive list of Mappings containing AMI IDs for every possible AWS region.

questions.explanation: AWS publishes public AMI IDs to Systems Manager Parameter Store. CloudFormation supports AWS-specific parameter types (such as `AWS::SSM::Parameter::Value<AWS::EC2::Image::Id>`), enabling templates to automatically resolve the correct regional AMI ID without hardcoding or maintaining manual mappings.

wrongOptionNotes.A: While a custom resource would work, it introduces unnecessary complexity and execution overhead when SSM Parameter Store already provides native AMI ID resolution.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Downloading AMI IDs from S3 requires maintaining an external synchronization mechanism, whereas AWS Systems Manager maintains official, automatically updated parameters.
wrongOptionNotes.D: While Mappings can store region-specific AMI IDs, hardcoding them requires manual updates whenever Amazon releases new AMI versions, making it inefficient compared to SSM parameters.

questions.question: A developer is configuring an AWS CodeBuild project to build a Java application that relies on corporate-internal Maven dependencies stored in an authenticating private repository. The build fails during the dependency download stage because CodeBuild cannot authenticate against the internal repository. Which approach should the developer use to securely provide the required credentials to the build process?

options.text: Pass the username and password as environment variables in plaintext directly within the AWS CodeBuild project configuration settings in the AWS Management Console.
Attach an Amazon EC2 instance profile containing the repository credentials to the CodeBuild project configuration.
Hardcode the credentials inside the settings.xml file of the Maven project and commit the file to the source code repository so CodeBuild can access it.

Store the credentials in AWS Secrets Manager, grant the CodeBuild service role permissions to read the secret, and retrieve the credentials dynamically within the buildspec.yml file before executing the Maven build.

questions.explanation: AWS CodeBuild can securely integrate with AWS Secrets Manager or AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. By granting the CodeBuild service role permissions to retrieve secrets at runtime, developers can inject credentials into environment variables or configuration files securely during the build phase.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Environment variables entered directly in the console can be viewed in plaintext by anyone with DescribeProjects permissions, posing a significant security risk.
wrongOptionNotes.B: CodeBuild runs in a managed container environment and does not support attaching EC2 instance profiles directly to projects.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Hardcoding credentials in source control violates basic security principles and leaks corporate credentials if the repository is compromised.

questions.question: An enterprise development team is using AWS Elastic Beanstalk to deploy a Python-based web application. The team notices that deployment updates frequently fail because the application takes a long time to warm up cache layers before it can handle incoming HTTP traffic successfully. Which Elastic Beanstalk configuration change will resolve this deployment issue?

options.text: Configure an appropriate health check URL path in the Elastic Beanstalk environment configuration so the load balancer waits for the application to return a healthy status before routing traffic.
Add a pre-deployment hook script that stops the application logging daemon.
Increase the deployment timeout limit in the AWS Elastic Beanstalk console without changing health check settings.
Switch the deployment policy from Rolling to All-at-once to speed up the transition and reduce overall deployment duration.

questions.explanation: Elastic Beanstalk integrates with Elastic Load Balancing health checks. By specifying a custom health check URL that only returns HTTP 200 after the cache is fully populated, the deployment process ensures that new instances are not marked as ready until they can actually handle production traffic.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Stopping logging daemons does not solve cache warmup issues or prevent premature traffic routing.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Merely increasing the timeout will cause the deployment to hang longer, but traffic will still hit the instances prematurely if the health check URL is not configured correctly.
wrongOptionNotes.D: An All-at-once deployment causes complete downtime and does not allow the instances to warm up before receiving traffic.

questions.question: A developer is implementing an AWS CloudFormation template to deploy an application infrastructure stack. The template creates an Amazon S3 bucket for logs. The developer wants to ensure that when the CloudFormation stack is deleted, the S3 bucket is also automatically deleted, even if the bucket contains objects. Which mechanism should the developer use?

options.text: Add the DeletionPolicy attribute set to Retain on the S3 bucket resource.
Configure the S3 bucket resource with the DeletionPolicy set to Delete and include an AWS::S3::BucketPolicy granting permissions.

Use an AWS CloudFormation custom resource or nested stack pattern that utilizes an S3 bucket with lifecycle policies or an explicit script to empty the bucket before stack deletion, or rely on a third-party macro.
Configure an AWS Lambda-backed custom resource that invokes an S3 batch operation to delete all objects upon stack deletion.

questions.explanation: Amazon S3 buckets must be empty before they can be deleted by AWS CloudFormation. Because CloudFormation's native DeletionPolicy: Delete fails on non-empty buckets, developers often use an AWS Lambda-backed custom resource to automatically empty the bucket during the stack deletion process.

wrongOptionNotes.A: The Retain deletion policy prevents the resource from being deleted when the stack is deleted, which is the opposite of the requirement.
wrongOptionNotes.B: By default, CloudFormation attempts to delete an S3 bucket when a stack is deleted, but deletion fails if the bucket is not empty, regardless of the default DeletionPolicy.
wrongOptionNotes.D: While a custom resource could achieve this, it adds unnecessary complexity and maintenance overhead compared to native CloudFormation features.

questions.question: A developer is configuring an AWS CodeDeploy deployment for a serverless application using an AWS Serverless Application Model (AWS SAM) template. The deployment strategy requires shifting 10% of traffic immediately, and the remaining 90% after a 10-minute linear interval. Which configuration property in the AWS SAM template achieves this requirement?

options.text: Configure an AWS CodeDeploy DeploymentGroup resource with a Linear10PercentEvery10Minutes deployment config inside the SAM template.
Set the AutoPublishAlias property to point to a CodeDeploy linear update configuration ARN.
Specify DeploymentPreference with Type set to Canary10Percent10Minutes under the AWS::Serverless::Function resource.
Specify DeploymentPreference with Type set to Linear10PercentEvery10Minutes under the AWS::Serverless::Function resource.

questions.explanation: AWS SAM simplifies serverless deployments by supporting pre-defined CodeDeploy deployment types via the DeploymentPreference property. Linear10PercentEvery10Minutes incrementally shifts traffic in 10% blocks over 10-minute intervals.

wrongOptionNotes.A: AWS SAM abstracts CodeDeploy configuration for serverless functions through the DeploymentPreference property on the function resource itself, rather than requiring an explicit DeploymentGroup resource.
wrongOptionNotes.B: AutoPublishAlias manages the alias pointing to the new version, but the traffic shifting strategy is defined inside the DeploymentPreference block.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Canary10Percent10Minutes shifts 10% of traffic, waits 10 minutes, and then shifts the remaining 90% all at once, rather than shifting linearly.

questions.question: A developer is building a CI/CD pipeline using AWS CodePipeline. The pipeline needs to build a Docker container image, tag it with the current Git commit hash, push the image to Amazon Elastic Container Registry (ECR), and then deploy it to Amazon ECS. Which buildspec.yml file structure should the developer use in the AWS CodeBuild stage to accomplish the tagging requirement?

options.text: Use the AWS CLI to query CloudTrail for the latest code commit event ID.
Use the built-in CodeBuild environment variable CODEBUILD_RESOLVED_SOURCE_VERSION to tag the Docker image during the build phase.
Execute a git log command inside the buildspec install phase to retrieve the commit hash and write it to a local text file.
Configure the CodePipeline action to automatically inject the commit hash as an environment variable named COMMIT_HASH.

questions.explanation: AWS CodeBuild provides environment variables such as CODEBUILD_RESOLVED_SOURCE_VERSION that automatically capture the commit hash of the source code being built. Developers can use this variable directly in buildspec commands to tag Docker images before pushing them to Amazon ECR.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Querying CloudTrail is inefficient, introduces latency, and requires overly permissive IAM roles.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Depending on the source provider and CodePipeline configuration, the local git repository history might be shallow or unavailable, making CODEBUILD_RESOLVED_SOURCE_VERSION a much more reliable choice.
wrongOptionNotes.D: CodePipeline does not automatically inject a variable named COMMIT_HASH into CodeBuild without explicit namespace configuration or environment variable parameter overrides.

questions.question: A developer is writing an AWS CloudFormation template that deploys an application stack across multiple AWS accounts and regions. The developer wants to reference an Amazon VPC ID created in a separate, centrally managed networking CloudFormation stack. What is the most robust and secure way to reference this VPC ID across stacks?

options.text: Read the VPC ID directly from the Amazon S3 template bucket using a dynamic reference.
Hardcode the VPC ID as a string parameter inside the CloudFormation template.
Use an AWS Lambda custom resource that queries the EC2 DescribeVpcs API during every stack update.
Export the VPC ID using CloudFormation Export and import it in the consuming stack using Fn::ImportValue.

questions.explanation: AWS CloudFormation allows data to be shared across stacks in the same AWS account and region by using the Output section with the Export attribute, and retrieving it in other stacks using the Fn::ImportValue intrinsic function.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Dynamic references support Secrets Manager and Systems Manager Parameter Store, not S3 bucket contents for cross-stack resource identifiers.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Hardcoding resource IDs breaks portability across different environments, accounts, and regions.
wrongOptionNotes.C: While a custom resource would work, it is over-engineered when native CloudFormation cross-stack references (Exports and Imports) are available.

questions.question: A development team is deploying a containerized application to Amazon ECS using the AWS Fargate launch type. The team needs to ensure that sensitive database connection strings are securely passed to the container at runtime without storing plaintext values in the ECS task definition file or source code. Which mechanism should the developer implement?

options.text: Reference the secret stored in AWS Secrets Manager using the secrets section of the container definition in the ECS task definition.
Pass the secret via the command override field in the ECS console when starting the task manually.
Store the database connection string in plaintext as an environment variable in the Dockerfile.
Write a custom entrypoint script inside the container that downloads the secret from an unauthenticated public S3 bucket.

questions.explanation: Amazon ECS task definitions allow seamless integration with AWS Secrets Manager and AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. By specifying the secrets mapping in the container definition, ECS automatically retrieves the secret and injects it into the container environment securely.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Command arguments appear in process lists and AWS CloudTrail logs in plaintext, failing security compliance.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Storing secrets in a Dockerfile exposes them in the image layers, which can be easily extracted and compromises security.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Storing secrets in an unauthenticated public S3 bucket is an extreme security vulnerability.

questions.question: An application deployed on AWS Elastic Beanstalk is experiencing intermittent failures. A developer needs to inspect the application logs and server error logs to troubleshoot the issue. Which action should the developer take to retrieve the most recent logs efficiently?

options.text: Modify the Elastic Beanstalk configuration to stream logs continuously to Amazon RDS.
Log into the AWS Elastic Beanstalk console and request either recent or full logs from the environment management dashboard, which bundles them into an Amazon S3 bucket.
Use SSH to connect directly to every single EC2 instance in the Auto Scaling group and manually copy log files via SCP.
Terminate the current environment and launch a new environment with debugging flags enabled.

questions.explanation: AWS Elastic Beanstalk simplifies log management by letting developers request log bundles directly through the console or CLI. Elastic Beanstalk aggregates logs from all instances in the environment and uploads them to an S3 bucket.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Amazon RDS is a relational database and cannot store streaming application log files directly.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Manually SSHing into individual instances is inefficient, not scalable, and often blocked if key pairs are not pre-configured.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Terminating the environment causes unnecessary downtime and destroys the logs needed for troubleshooting current errors.

questions.question: A developer is configuring an AWS CodePipeline pipeline that builds and packages a serverless application. The developer wants to ensure that automated integration tests run against the packaged AWS SAM application template before the pipeline proceeds to the production deployment stage. Which action should the developer take?

options.text: Configure an Amazon CloudWatch alarm to trigger a rollback if production invocation errors exceed a threshold.
Add an AWS CodeBuild action stage after the build stage that executes test scripts using the AWS SAM CLI local emulation features.
Configure an approval action that requires a manual human click to verify integration tests.
Attach an AWS Lambda function directly to the Amazon S3 artifact bucket to execute tests asynchronously.

questions.explanation: AWS CodePipeline allows developers to insert custom testing stages. By using AWS CodeBuild with the AWS SAM CLI installed, developers can run local unit and integration tests against serverless templates and code before deploying to live environments.

wrongOptionNotes.A: CloudWatch alarms handle post-deployment monitoring and rollback, not pre-deployment integration testing.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Manual approvals rely on human intervention rather than automated integration testing.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Attaching an S3 trigger to test packaged artifacts can cause race conditions and does not properly sequence stages within the CodePipeline execution flow.

questions.question: A developer is writing an AWS CloudFormation template that deploys an Amazon DynamoDB table. The developer needs to ensure that table naming follows a strict convention based on the deployment stage (e.g., prod-users, dev-users) passed as a parameter. How can the developer accomplish this dynamically within the template?

options.text: Use the Fn::GetAtt intrinsic function to retrieve the name of the stage parameter.
Hardcode the table name using an environment variable injected by the AWS CLI during deployment.
Use the CloudFormation Fn::Sub intrinsic function to combine the stage parameter with a static suffix.
Use Python code inside the CloudFormation YAML template to evaluate conditional string concatenation.

questions.explanation: CloudFormation intrinsic functions such as Fn::Sub are designed to substitute variables into template strings. This allows developers to construct dynamic resource names by combining input parameters with static strings.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Fn::GetAtt retrieves attributes from existing deployed resources, not parameters passed into a template.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Hardcoding defeats parameterization and does not leverage CloudFormation's native parameter capabilities.
wrongOptionNotes.D: CloudFormation templates do not execute embedded Python code; they use built-in intrinsic functions.

questions.question: A developer is managing an application deployed on Amazon ECS using the EC2 launch type. The application is updated frequently via AWS CodeDeploy using a blue/green deployment strategy. During a deployment, the developer notices that old container instances are terminated too quickly, cutting off long-polling client connections. Which CodeDeploy setting should the developer adjust?

options.text: Configure the terminationwaitbytime in the CodeDeploy deployment group configuration to introduce a delay before terminating original instances.
Increase the maximum container memory limit in the ECS task definition.
Switch the ECS deployment controller from CodeDeploy to ECS rolling update.
Modify the AWS Auto Scaling group cooldown period to a higher value.

questions.explanation: In AWS CodeDeploy blue/green deployments for Amazon ECS or EC2, developers can specify a waiting period before terminating the original instances. This ensures that in-flight requests or long-polling connections complete successfully before the old infrastructure is destroyed.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Container memory limits govern resource consumption, not connection draining or instance termination grace periods.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Switching to a rolling update does not solve the underlying abrupt termination issue and abandons the blue/green strategy.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Auto Scaling group cooldown periods manage scaling policies, not CodeDeploy blue/green instance lifecycle termination hooks.

questions.question: A developer is configuring an AWS CodeBuild project to build and test a Node.js application. The project requires downloading numerous npm modules from the internet for every build, resulting in long build durations. Which optimization technique should the developer implement to reduce build times?

options.text: Enable local caching in the CodeBuild project configuration targeting the npm cache directory (node_modules or ~/.npm).
Package all node_modules inside the source code repository and commit them to AWS CodeCommit.
Increase the compute type of the CodeBuild project from BUILD_GENERAL1_SMALL to BUILD_GENERAL1_LARGE.
Set up a NAT Gateway with higher bandwidth limits in the VPC.

questions.explanation: AWS CodeBuild supports caching to store frequently used data on local storage or in Amazon S3 for reuse across builds. Enabling local caching for the npm cache directory avoids redownloading dependencies on every build.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Committing node_modules bloats the repository size, slows down git operations, and is an anti-pattern.
wrongOptionNotes.C: While a larger compute type increases CPU and memory, it does not solve network latency or redundant package downloading as efficiently as caching.
wrongOptionNotes.D: CodeBuild runs in AWS-managed VPCs by default unless explicitly configured otherwise; adjusting a NAT gateway will not cache npm packages.

questions.question: A developer is using AWS CloudFormation to manage a multi-tier web application. The application stack frequently fails during updates because a dependent relational database takes time to initialize after creation. How can the developer ensure that CloudFormation waits for the database to be fully available before proceeding to create dependant resources?

options.text: Wrap the database resource in an Amazon S3 bucket notification event.
Set the TimeoutInMinutes parameter of the CloudFormation stack to zero.
Use the DependsOn attribute combined with an AWS CloudFormation WaitCondition or a custom resource that polls the database until it responds.
Add a pre-install script directly inside the AWS IAM role policy document.

questions.explanation: While CloudFormation creates resources in parallel where possible, developers can enforce sequential creation using the DependsOn attribute. For resources like databases that require time to initialize past their API creation, combining DependsOn with WaitConditions or Lambda-backed custom resources ensures proper synchronization.

wrongOptionNotes.A: S3 bucket notifications respond to object creations, not database initialization states.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Setting the timeout to zero causes immediate failure or disables timeout tracking incorrectly.
wrongOptionNotes.D: IAM role policies define permissions and cannot execute installation scripts or control stack creation order.

questions.question: An enterprise development team uses AWS Elastic Beanstalk to run a mission-critical web application. The team wants to test a new version of the application with live production traffic without impacting existing users, and wants the ability to rollback instantly if errors occur. Which Elastic Beanstalk deployment method should the team choose?

options.text: Enable mutable instance updates via direct SSH modifications.
Use Rolling with additional batch deployment policy.
Use an All-at-once deployment policy to replace all instances simultaneously.
Configure a Blue/Green deployment using a CNAME swap or an AWS CodePipeline integration with Elastic Beanstalk environment cloning.

questions.explanation: Elastic Beanstalk facilitates blue/green deployments by allowing developers to create a separate clone environment for the new application version. Once tested, traffic can be seamlessly switched between environments using a CNAME swap with zero downtime.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Manual SSH modifications are not reproducible, violate immutable infrastructure principles, and offer no instant rollback.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Rolling deployments update batches of live instances gradually, which exposes live users to the new version without an easy way to isolate test traffic.
wrongOptionNotes.C: All-at-once causes downtime and provides no mechanism for immediate traffic splitting or safe testing.

questions.question: A developer is configuring an AWS CodePipeline pipeline that builds a static React frontend application and deploys it to an Amazon S3 bucket. The developer notices that after deployment, users report seeing outdated content due to browser caching. Which step should the developer add to the pipeline to fix this issue?

options.text: Change the default index document of the S3 bucket on every deployment.
Delete and recreate the Amazon S3 bucket during every pipeline execution.
Enable versioning on the Amazon S3 bucket and configure Object Lock.
Add an AWS CodeBuild action after the S3 deployment that executes an AWS CLI command to create an Amazon CloudFront cache invalidation.

questions.explanation: When deploying static web applications hosted on S3 and distributed via Amazon CloudFront, new deployments require clearing the edge cache. Adding a CloudFront cache invalidation step using the AWS CLI in a CodeBuild or deployment action ensures users receive the updated assets immediately.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Changing the index document name is unnecessary and breaks static website routing.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Recreating the S3 bucket is destructive, slow, and does not address edge caching mechanisms like CloudFront.
wrongOptionNotes.C: S3 versioning and Object Lock protect against accidental deletion and preserve history, but do not automatically clear edge or browser caches.

questions.question: A developer is configuring an AWS CodeDeploy deployment for an application running on an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group. The deployment configuration must ensure that during a deployment, the minimum number of healthy instances available to serve traffic never drops below 75% of the desired capacity, while allowing the deployment to finish as quickly as possible. Which deployment configuration meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a custom deployment configuration with a minimum healthy hosts type of FLEET_PERCENT set to 75.
Create a custom deployment configuration with a minimum healthy hosts type of HOST_COUNT set to 1 instance.
Use the CodeDeployDefault.OneAtATime configuration to ensure minimal disruption to the existing fleet.
Use the CodeDeployDefault.AllAtOnce configuration to achieve the fastest possible deployment speed.

questions.explanation: AWS CodeDeploy allows you to define deployment configurations that control the speed and safety of deployments.
