options.text: Use CloudFormation Mappings combined with the Fn::FindInMap intrinsic function and AWS::Region pseudo parameter.
Deploy the exact same template without modification, trusting that AWS services will automatically translate region-specific AMIs.
Hardcode the us-east-1 resource identifiers directly into the main CloudFormation template and write a bash script to replace them during us-west-2 deployment.
Store all AMI IDs in plain text files inside an Amazon S3 bucket and have Lambda parse them at runtime.

questions.explanation: CloudFormation Mappings provide a structured way to conditionally select region-specific configuration values, such as AMIs, based on the AWS::Region pseudo parameter during multi-region deployments.

wrongOptionNotes.B: AMI IDs are strictly region-specific; attempting to use an us-east-1 AMI ID in us-west-2 will result in a deployment failure.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Hardcoding and using custom bash scripts defeats the declarative benefits of CloudFormation and introduces deployment errors.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Relying on external Lambda parsing for infrastructure parameters adds unnecessary complexity and latency to stack creation.

questions.question: A developer is troubleshooting a multi-region application where data written to an Amazon S3 bucket in us-east-1 is replicated to us-west-2. Users in us-west-2 report that occasionally, newly replicated objects return 'Access Denied' errors when fetched. An investigation reveals that the objects are encrypted with a customer-managed KMS key. What is the root cause of this error?

options.text: Cross-region replication does not support KMS-encrypted objects and silently corrupts the ciphertext.
Amazon S3 Cross-Region Replication automatically deletes KMS keys after 24 hours for security compliance.
The destination bucket policy explicitly denies access to KMS keys from other AWS accounts.
The IAM role configured for S3 replication lacks permissions to decrypt objects using the source KMS key or encrypt them using the destination KMS key.

questions.explanation: S3 replication of KMS-encrypted objects requires that the IAM role used by S3 has explicit permissions to use both the source KMS key (for decryption) and the destination KMS key (for encryption).

wrongOptionNotes.A: S3 replication fully supports KMS encryption; failures or access errors are strictly permission-based.
wrongOptionNotes.B: AWS KMS keys are never automatically deleted by S3 replication.
wrongOptionNotes.C: If the bucket policy denied access entirely, replication itself would fail rather than intermittent read errors.

questions.question: A media company runs a content management system on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer in us-east-1. For disaster recovery, a warm standby environment is maintained in us-west-2. The development team needs to ensure that user session data stored in an Amazon DynamoDB table is consistently accessible across both regions without manual intervention. Which architecture should be deployed?

options.text: Configure DynamoDB global tables spanning us-east-1 and us-west-2.
Configure an AWS Lambda function in us-west-2 to poll the us-east-1 DynamoDB table every minute.
Take daily point-in-time recovery (PITR) backups in us-east-1 and restore them manually in us-west-2 during a disaster.
Use Amazon S3 event notifications to export session items as JSON files to us-west-2.

questions.explanation: DynamoDB global tables provide a fully managed multi-region replication solution, making them ideal for maintaining synchronized session states in warm standby and disaster recovery architectures.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Polling via Lambda introduces high latency, high read costs, and is inefficient compared to native database replication.
wrongOptionNotes.C: PITR restores take time, resulting in an unacceptably high RTO for warm standby session management.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Exporting session files as JSON to S3 does not maintain a transactional, low-latency database state for active user sessions.

questions.question: A developer is deploying a containerized application on Amazon ECS across us-east-1 and us-west-2. The application configuration values are stored in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. During a disaster recovery drill, the application in us-west-2 failed to start because it could not retrieve its parameters. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: AWS Systems Manager automatically deletes parameters that are not accessed within 30 days.
Parameter Store requires all values to be encrypted with a global KMS key that is disabled by default.
ECS tasks running on Fargate are prohibited from reading Parameter Store values across regions.
Parameter Store parameters are region-specific, and the parameters were only created in us-east-1.

questions.explanation: Systems Manager Parameter Store is a regional service. For multi-region architectures and disaster recovery readiness, configuration parameters must be deployed and maintained across all target regions.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Systems Manager parameters persist indefinitely until explicitly deleted.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Standard parameters can be stored as plain strings without KMS encryption, and KMS keys are enabled by default.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Tasks can read parameters from other regions if explicitly configured with the correct region SDK client, though best practice dictates replicating parameters to all target regions.

questions.question: An application hosted on AWS Elastic Beanstalk in us-east-1 connects to an Amazon Aurora database. The engineering team is designing a disaster recovery plan and needs to ensure that if us-east-1 suffers a major failure, the Elastic Beanstalk environment can be rapidly provisioned in us-west-2 and connected to the Aurora read replica. Which approach provides the most efficient deployment automation?

options.text: Manually recreate the Elastic Beanstalk environment using the AWS Management Console during the outage.
Store the Elastic Beanstalk environment configuration as an application version and use AWS CloudFormation or the EB CLI to deploy the stack in us-west-2.
Configure Elastic Beanstalk to automatically mirror instances across regions without user intervention.
Take an image of the Elastic Beanstalk EC2 instances and copy the AMI to us-east-2.

questions.explanation: Using Infrastructure as Code (IaC) such as AWS CloudFormation or Elastic Beanstalk configuration templates ensures that secondary disaster recovery environments can be spun up quickly and reliably in alternate regions.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Manual console creation is slow, error-prone, and increases RTO significantly.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Elastic Beanstalk environments are single-region constructs; they do not automatically mirror themselves across regions.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Elastic Beanstalk manages instance provisioning dynamically; copying AMIs manually does not recreate the managed platform configuration or environment settings.

questions.question: A developer is architecting a disaster recovery strategy for a static website hosted in an Amazon S3 bucket in us-east-1, backed by a secondary bucket in us-west-2. The frontend is delivered via Amazon CloudFront. The developer wants CloudFront to automatically route requests to the secondary S3 bucket if the primary S3 bucket returns 5xx server error codes. How should this be implemented?

options.text: Enable S3 Cross-Region Replication and rely on S3 bucket name aliasing.
Write a custom AWS Lambda function to intercept all S3 GET requests and retry against the secondary bucket upon failure.
Configure Amazon Route 53 to check the S3 HTTP endpoint and switch DNS records.
Configure CloudFront with an Origin Group containing both S3 buckets as origins, and set the failover criteria to HTTP 5xx error codes.

questions.explanation: CloudFront Origin Groups provide built-in failover capabilities for static and dynamic origins, enabling seamless redirection to a secondary S3 bucket when the primary bucket returns server errors.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Replication copies data, but it does not provide automatic HTTP-level failover handling for client requests if the primary endpoint goes down.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Using Lambda@Edge for basic origin failover adds unnecessary execution costs and complexity compared to native CloudFront Origin Groups.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Route 53 health checks cannot directly inspect S3 static website error status codes to drive DNS failover for CloudFront origins.

questions.question: An application running on an Amazon EC2 instance needs to invoke an AWS Lambda function. To adhere to security best practices, the developer wants to ensure the EC2 instance can only invoke this specific Lambda function and no other AWS resources. Which combination of configurations must the developer implement?

options.text: Attach an IAM role to the EC2 instance with administrator access, and configure an Amazon API Gateway endpoint in front of the Lambda function.
Store the AWS credentials of a dedicated IAM user inside the EC2 instance memory and use the AWS SDK to invoke the Lambda function.
Configure the Lambda function's resource-based policy to allow the EC2 instance ID, and attach an empty IAM policy to the EC2 instance.

Attach an IAM instance profile to the EC2 instance with an IAM policy granting lambda:InvokeFunction on the specific Lambda function ARN, and ensure the Lambda function has no resource-based policy restricting access.

questions.explanation: To allow an EC2 instance to interact securely with other AWS services, developers should attach an IAM role via an instance profile. The policy attached to the role must restrict actions to the specific resource ARN required, avoiding broad wildcard permissions.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Using administrator access violates the principle of least privilege, and API Gateway introduces unnecessary overhead when an EC2 instance can invoke Lambda directly.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Hardcoding or storing long-term IAM user credentials on an EC2 instance is a severe anti-pattern and security risk.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Lambda resource-based policies cannot reference EC2 instance IDs as principals; they require IAM roles or users.

questions.question: A developer is configuring an Amazon API Gateway HTTP API that integrates with an AWS Lambda backend. The API must validate incoming JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) issued by an external identity provider before invoking the Lambda function. Which configuration should the developer choose to meet this requirement natively?

options.text: Use an Amazon Cognito user pool authorizer, which is the only type of authorizer supported by API Gateway HTTP APIs.
Configure an AWS IAM authorizer and require clients to sign every HTTP request using Signature Version 4.
Write custom code inside the backend Lambda function to decode and verify the cryptographic signature of the JWT header.
Configure a native JWT authorizer directly within API Gateway by providing the issuer URL and audience.

questions.explanation: API Gateway HTTP APIs natively support JWT authorizers (JSON Web Token validation), which offload token validation (checking signature, expiration, issuer, and audience) completely from the backend application code.

wrongOptionNotes.A: API Gateway HTTP APIs support any valid OIDC-compliant JWT issuer, not just Amazon Cognito user pools.
wrongOptionNotes.B: External identity providers issue standard JWTs, not SigV4 authorization headers, making IAM authorizers inappropriate for third-party token validation.
wrongOptionNotes.C: While technically possible, validating JWTs inside Lambda wastes execution time and invokes the function for unauthorized requests, making it an anti-pattern.

questions.question: A developer needs to secure sensitive database passwords used by an AWS Lambda function. The passwords must be automatically rotated every 30 days without modifying the Lambda function code or redeploying it. Where should the credentials be stored, and how should rotation be achieved?

options.text: Store the password in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store as a SecureString and write a custom cron job on an EC2 instance to update it.
Store the password in AWS Secrets Manager and configure its built-in rotation feature using an AWS Lambda rotation function.
Store the password in an Amazon S3 bucket with server-side encryption and use S3 object versioning for rotation.
Store the password as environment variables in the Lambda function configuration and update them via a CloudFormation template every 30 days.

questions.explanation: AWS Secrets Manager is designed for managing and automatically rotating database credentials, API keys, and other secrets. It features built-in integration with AWS Lambda to rotate credentials automatically on a schedule.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Parameter Store does not have native automated rotation workflows like Secrets Manager, requiring custom infrastructure management.
wrongOptionNotes.C: S3 buckets do not provide credential lifecycle management or automated rotation capabilities.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Updating environment variables requires redeploying the Lambda function, which causes downtime and fails the requirement for zero code modification.

questions.question: A developer is writing an AWS Lambda function that retrieves sensitive configuration data from AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. The parameter was created as a SecureString using a custom AWS KMS customer managed key (CMK). When the Lambda function runs, it throws an AccessDeniedException. What is the most likely cause of this error?

options.text: The Lambda function is missing an Amazon VPC endpoint for AWS Systems Manager.
Systems Manager parameters stored as SecureString cannot be accessed by AWS Lambda functions under any circumstances.
The IAM execution role of the Lambda function lacks permissions for kms:Decrypt on the specific customer managed key, and ssm:GetParameter on the parameter.
The parameter value exceeds the 4 KB size limit enforced by Parameter Store standard tiers.

questions.explanation: Accessing a SecureString parameter encrypted with a custom KMS key requires the caller's IAM role to have both `ssm:GetParameter` on the parameter resource and `kms:Decrypt` on the associated KMS key policy.

wrongOptionNotes.A: While VPC endpoints may be needed for isolated subnets, an AccessDeniedException specifically points to IAM authorization or KMS policy failures rather than network connectivity.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Lambda functions can access SecureString parameters provided their IAM role has the necessary permissions.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Size limit violations throw ParameterLimitExceeded or validation exceptions, not AccessDeniedException.

questions.question: An enterprise application hosted on Amazon ECS uses AWS Fargate. The application needs to read configuration parameters from AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store and secrets from AWS Secrets Manager during startup. How should the developer securely inject these values into the container without exposing them in plaintext within the task definition file?

options.text: Store the secrets in an Amazon S3 bucket with public read access and have the application download them via HTTP.
Reference the Parameter Store parameters and Secrets Manager secrets using the 'secrets' section of the ECS container definition, mapping them to environment variables.
Hardcode the secrets and parameters directly into the container's Dockerfile during the CI/CD build stage.
Write a shell script inside the container entrypoint that uses AWS CLI to download secrets, and store the AWS root account credentials in plain text environment variables.

questions.explanation: Amazon ECS allows container definitions to securely inject secrets and parameters from Secrets Manager or Systems Manager Parameter Store directly into the container environment variables at runtime, referencing their ARNs or parameter names.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Using public S3 buckets for secrets exposes sensitive data to the entire internet.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Hardcoding secrets into container images is a major security vulnerability because anyone with image read access can extract them.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Storing root credentials and executing CLI calls inside entrypoints increases attack surface and violates security best practices.

questions.question: A developer is configuring an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of an Amazon S3 bucket. To prevent users from bypassing CloudFront and accessing the S3 bucket directly via its public URL, what configuration must be implemented?

options.text: Add a custom HTTP header in CloudFront and configure an AWS WAF rule on the S3 bucket to inspect the header.
Set the S3 bucket policy to deny all traffic except requests originating from the developer's corporate public IP address.
Enable public read access on the S3 bucket and obfuscate the bucket URL so users cannot guess it.
Configure Origin Access Control (OAC) on the CloudFront distribution and update the S3 bucket policy to allow only the OAC principal.

questions.explanation: Origin Access Control (OAC) restricts access to an S3 bucket so that only Amazon CloudFront can read the objects. The S3 bucket can then block all public access while CloudFront signs requests using SigV4.

wrongOptionNotes.A: S3 buckets do not natively support AWS WAF rule inspection or custom header evaluation at the bucket level without Lambda@Edge or CloudFront Functions.
wrongOptionNotes.B: This blocks legitimate end-users whose traffic flows through CloudFront edge locations, breaking application functionality.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Obfuscation through unguessable URLs (security through obscurity) is not a valid security control; S3 objects remain publicly accessible.

questions.question: A developer is building an application that generates signed URLs for private objects stored in an Amazon S3 bucket using the AWS SDK. The application runs on AWS Lambda. The generated URLs must expire after exactly 60 seconds. When testing, the developer notices that some clients report expired URLs immediately upon receipt. What is the most probable cause?

options.text: Amazon S3 enforces a minimum expiration time of 3600 seconds (1 hour) for all presigned URLs.
Presigned URLs can only be generated by Amazon EC2 instance metadata services, not Lambda execution roles.
Time synchronization drift between the client device and AWS services, or the Lambda function execution environment clock.
The AWS SDK automatically invalidates presigned URLs if they are generated inside an AWS Lambda function.

questions.explanation: Presigned URLs incorporate AWS Signature Version 4, which embeds a timestamp. If there is clock skew between the generating entity, AWS, and the client consuming the URL, validation errors occur. Setting very short expiration windows (like 60 seconds) amplifies the impact of clock skew.

wrongOptionNotes.A: S3 presigned URLs can expire in as little as 1 second, with a maximum expiration limit of 7 days (when using IAM credentials).
wrongOptionNotes.B: Presigned URLs can be generated by any valid AWS credentials, including IAM roles assumed by Lambda functions.
wrongOptionNotes.D: AWS Lambda functions can generate valid presigned URLs without automatic invalidation by the SDK.

questions.question: A developer is configuring cross-account access for an Amazon S3 bucket located in Account A. An application running in Account B needs to read and write objects to this bucket. Which combination of policies is strictly required to establish this access securely?

options.text: An S3 bucket policy in Account A allowing public read and write access, with no IAM policies required in Account B.
An IAM policy in Account B attached to the application's role granting permissions on the bucket, and an S3 bucket policy in Account A granting access to Account B's role.
Enabling cross-account sharing via AWS Trusted Advisor in Account A.
An IAM policy in Account A attached to the S3 bucket, with no policies needed in Account B.

questions.explanation: Cross-account access in AWS requires a 'two-way' evaluation. Both the resource-based policy (S3 bucket policy in the owner account) and the identity-based policy (IAM policy in the calling account) must explicitly allow the action.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Making an S3 bucket publicly writable is a catastrophic security vulnerability and violates all compliance standards.
wrongOptionNotes.C: AWS Trusted Advisor provides recommendations and checks, but does not configure access permissions.
wrongOptionNotes.D: IAM policies cannot be attached directly to S3 buckets; resource policies on S3 are called bucket policies, and cross-account principals still require IAM permission.

questions.question: An application hosted on AWS Lambda connects to an Amazon RDS MySQL database. The database credentials are stored in AWS Secrets Manager. During peak traffic hours, the Lambda function reports intermittent connection timeouts and throttling errors related to calling Secrets Manager. How should the developer resolve this issue efficiently without compromising security?

options.text: Hardcode the database credentials as plaintext environment variables in the Lambda function configuration.
Increase the Lambda function timeout limit to 15 minutes.
Modify the Lambda function code to cache the retrieved secret locally within the execution context outside the handler function.
Disable AWS CloudTrail logging for Secrets Manager to speed up API responses.

questions.explanation: Lambda execution environments persist across warm invocations. By retrieving and caching secrets outside the handler function, developers can significantly reduce API calls to Secrets Manager, eliminating throttling and improving performance.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Hardcoding credentials violates security best practices by exposing sensitive data in the function configuration.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Increasing the function timeout does not address API rate limiting or throttling caused by repeatedly fetching secrets on every invocation.
wrongOptionNotes.D: CloudTrail logging is asynchronous and does not impact Secrets Manager API latency or cause client-side throttling.

questions.question: A developer is writing a Python application using the AWS SDK for Python (Boto3) to assume an IAM role in another AWS account. The application runs on an Amazon EC2 instance. When executing the assume_role API call, the application receives a ClientError. What is the most likely configuration error?

options.text: The AWS region configured in Boto3 does not match the region where the IAM role was created.
The IAM role being assumed lacks a trust policy that explicitly permits the EC2 instance's IAM role to perform sts:AssumeRole.
The EC2 instance metadata service version 1 (IMDSv1) is disabled on the instance.
The target IAM role has an active MFA device enforced, but no MFA token was passed in the API call.

questions.explanation: Role assumption requires two permissions: the calling entity must have `sts:AssumeRole` allowed in its identity policy, and the target role must trust the caller via its trust policy (resource-based policy for the role).

wrongOptionNotes.A: IAM is a global service, so role assumption via AWS STS does not depend on specific regional endpoints.
wrongOptionNotes.C: IMDSv1 or IMDSv2 configuration affects local credential retrieval, not cross-account role assumption logic.
wrongOptionNotes.D: While MFA can cause errors if required, the most fundamental and common omission in cross-account assumption is the missing trust relationship.

questions.question: An enterprise application stores sensitive compliance logs in an Amazon S3 bucket. Security mandates that all objects written to this bucket must be encrypted using server-side encryption with customer-managed keys (SSE-KMS), and any unencrypted upload attempts must be outright rejected. Which bucket policy statement enforces this requirement?

options.text: A bucket policy with a Deny effect on s3:PutObject when s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption does not equal aws:kms.
Configuring an AWS WAF web ACL on the S3 bucket to inspect PUT requests for encryption headers.
A bucket policy with an Allow effect on s3:PutObject only when s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption equals AES256.
Enabling default encryption on the S3 bucket using Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3).

questions.explanation: To strictly enforce compliance requirements like mandatory SSE-KMS encryption, developers must use an explicit `Deny` condition in the S3 bucket policy that triggers if the `s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption` header is missing or does not match `aws:kms`.

wrongOptionNotes.B: S3 buckets do not support direct attachment of AWS WAF web ACLs.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Allow policies alone are prone to override misconfigurations and AES256 specifies S3-managed keys (SSE-S3), not customer-managed KMS keys.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Default encryption automatically encrypts unencrypted uploads, but it does not block clients from explicitly supplying alternative encryption headers or weaker encryption methods unless enforced via a Deny policy.

questions.question: A developer is configuring an Amazon API Gateway REST API backed by an AWS Lambda function. The application is experiencing a high volume of requests from malicious clients attempting credential stuffing and brute-force attacks. Which AWS service should the developer integrate with API Gateway to inspect web traffic and block these malicious requests at the edge?

options.text: AWS WAF (Web Application Firewall)
Amazon GuardDuty
AWS Shield Advanced
Amazon Inspector

questions.explanation: AWS WAF lets you monitor HTTP and HTTPS requests forwarded to an Amazon API Gateway REST API, CloudFront distribution, or Application Load Balancer, and allows you to control access based on conditions such as IP addresses, SQL injection, and rate limiting.

wrongOptionNotes.B: GuardDuty is a threat detection service that monitors AWS CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and DNS logs, not real-time inline API gateway HTTP traffic blocking.
wrongOptionNotes.C: AWS Shield protects against large-scale network and transport layer DDoS attacks (Layer 3 and 4), whereas WAF protects against application layer (Layer 7) threats like brute force.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Amazon Inspector performs automated security vulnerability assessments on EC2 instances, container images, and Lambda functions.

questions.question: A developer is writing an AWS Lambda function that needs to generate cryptographic signatures using an asymmetric Customer Managed Key (CMK) stored in AWS KMS. The function has been granted kms:Sign permissions. During execution, the function fails with an error indicating that the key usage is invalid. What is the root cause of this error?

options.text: Lambda execution roles are prohibited from calling cryptographic operations on KMS keys.
The KMS key is symmetric, and symmetric keys cannot be used in AWS Lambda functions.
The KMS key policy lacks an explicit Deny statement for public access.
The KMS key was created with a Key Usage of ENCRYPT_DECRYPT instead of SIGN_VERIFY.

questions.explanation: When creating an asymmetric KMS key in AWS KMS, you must define its Key Usage: either `ENCRYPT_DECRYPT` or `SIGN_VERIFY`. Attempting to call `kms:Sign` on a key configured for `ENCRYPT_DECRYPT` results in an invalid key usage error.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Lambda execution roles can call KMS APIs provided they have explicit IAM policy permissions.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Symmetric keys can be used in Lambda for encryption and decryption, but signing requires specific asymmetric key configurations.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Lack of a Deny statement does not cause a key usage validation error.

questions.question: A developer is configuring an IAM policy for an application running on AWS Lambda. The application needs to read and write items to a specific Amazon DynamoDB table named 'UserOrders', but must not be permitted to modify table schemas or delete tables. Which IAM policy correctly implements this least-privilege requirement?

options.text: Actions include dynamodb:GetItem, dynamodb:PutItem, dynamodb:UpdateItem, dynamodb:DeleteItem, dynamodb:Query, and dynamodb:Scan, with the Resource ARN set to the specific table ARN.
Actions include dynamodb:DeleteItem and dynamodb:CreateTable, with the Resource set to '*'.
An IAM policy granting administrator access, as DynamoDB tables are secured via table-level tags rather than IAM.
Action set to dynamodb:* with the Resource ARN set to the 'UserOrders' table ARN.

questions.explanation: To adhere to the principle of least privilege, IAM policies for database interactions should scope permissions to specific data-plane actions (e.g., `GetItem`, `PutItem`, `Query`) rather than wildcard actions (`dynamodb:*`), and restrict the resource ARN to the specific table.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Setting the resource to '*' and including CreateTable violates the principle of least privilege completely.
wrongOptionNotes.C: DynamoDB permissions are strictly controlled via IAM policies and resource-based policies, not tags alone.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Using dynamodb:* grants administrative control-plane permissions (such as DeleteTable) even when scoped to a specific table ARN.

questions.question: An application running on an Amazon EC2 instance needs to read and write objects in an Amazon S3 bucket. During troubleshooting, the developer notices a 403 Access Denied error when the application attempts to execute the PutObject API call. The bucket policy denies public access, but allows the instance role. What is the most likely root cause?

options.text: The Amazon EC2 instance security group outbound rules are blocking traffic on port 443.
The Amazon S3 bucket does not have Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) configured for PUT requests.
The Amazon S3 bucket is located in a different AWS Region than the EC2 instance, causing a routing failure.
The EC2 instance is missing an Attached IAM instance profile that grants permissions to the specific S3 bucket.

questions.explanation: Applications running on Amazon EC2 rely on IAM roles associated via an instance profile to obtain temporary AWS credentials through the instance metadata service (IMDS). A 403 Access Denied error explicitly points to missing or insufficient IAM permissions.

wrongOptionNotes.A: By default, security groups allow all outbound traffic. Even if restricted, port 443 is needed for HTTPS, but a network block would result in connection timeouts, not a 403 Access Denied error.
wrongOptionNotes.B: CORS errors only affect browser-based client applications making cross-origin requests, not backend applications running directly on EC2 instances.
wrongOptionNotes.C: S3 is a global namespace with regional endpoints; cross-region S3 API calls succeed as long as network routing and permissions are correct.

questions.question: A developer is configuring an AWS Lambda function to connect to an Amazon RDS database located in a private subnet. When the Lambda function is invoked, it consistently times out without establishing a connection. The RDS database security group allows ingress on port 3306 from the Lambda security group. What could be causing this production failure?

options.text: AWS Lambda does not support connecting to MySQL databases residing in private subnets.
The Lambda execution role lacks permissions to invoke Amazon RDS APIs.
The Lambda function is not configured with a VPC configuration, subnet IDs, and security groups matching the private RDS subnets.
The RDS instance is configured with a public IP address which prevents private subnet routing.

questions.explanation: Lambda functions deployed without VPC configurations execute in an AWS-managed VPC and cannot access resources in a private customer VPC. Connecting to private database subnets requires attaching the Lambda function to the VPC.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Lambda fully supports connecting to relational databases in private VPC subnets provided network routing (NAT Gateway or VPC endpoints) and security groups are correct.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Standard database connections use network TCP traffic and database credentials, not AWS IAM API calls to RDS, unless using IAM database authentication.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Having a public IP or not does not prevent internal private routing within a VPC or security group rules from functioning properly.

questions.question: A developer is troubleshooting an AWS CloudFormation stack update failure. An IAM policy resource defined in the template fails to update because of a malformed JSON syntax error. Which action should the developer take to diagnose the exact syntax violation?

options.text: Restart the AWS Systems Manager Agent on the target resource to force a policy re-evaluation.
Review the VPC Flow Logs for the region to trace where the JSON validation packet was dropped.
Check AWS CloudTrail logs for IAM API call failures made by the CloudFormation service role.
Inspect the CloudFormation stack events console for detailed failure reasons, or validate the template locally using the AWS CLI cfn-lint tool.

questions.explanation: CloudFormation template validation and syntax errors are captured in stack failure events. Local tools such as cfn-lint or the AWS CLI validate-template command help isolate structural issues before deployment.

wrongOptionNotes.A: SSM Agent has no role in parsing or validating CloudFormation templates or IAM policy syntax.
wrongOptionNotes.B: VPC Flow Logs capture IP traffic metadata and are entirely unrelated to template syntax validation.
wrongOptionNotes.C: CloudTrail records API calls, but syntax validation failures happen before API calls are dispatched to IAM, as the template itself is malformed.

questions.question: A web application running on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate attempts to download configuration files from an encrypted Amazon S3 bucket using a customer managed AWS KMS key. The task fails to start, throwing an error indicating the key is inaccessible. What is the missing configuration?

options.text: The ECS task execution role lacks permissions to call kms:Decrypt on the specific KMS customer managed key.
The Amazon ECS cluster security group must allow inbound traffic on port 443 from the KMS service endpoint.
The S3 bucket policy must explicitly trust the AWS KMS service principal.
The ECS container instance IAM role must be added to the Amazon S3 bucket access control list.

questions.explanation: When AWS services interact with resources encrypted by a KMS customer managed key (CMK), both the IAM policy of the calling identity (ECS task execution role) and the KMS key policy must grant access permissions.

wrongOptionNotes.B: KMS calls are outbound HTTPS requests initiated by the container/task runtime, which security groups allow by default.
wrongOptionNotes.C: KMS keys protect data; S3 buckets need bucket policies or IAM permissions allowing decryption, but KMS key policies also need to trust the IAM role performing the decryption.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Fargate uses task execution roles rather than container instance IAM roles (since Fargate manages the underlying instances), and ACLs are deprecated in favor of IAM policies.

questions.question: A developer is writing an AWS Lambda function that retrieves database credentials stored securely in AWS Secrets Manager. During execution, the function throws a ResourceNotFoundException. What is the most probable cause of this error?

options.text: The AWS KMS key used to encrypt the secret has been scheduled for deletion.
The Lambda execution role lacks the secretsmanager:GetSecretValue permission, or the secret name/ARN provided in the code is incorrect.
The secret has expired and needs to be manually rotated via an Amazon SNS notification.
The Lambda function is missing a VPC endpoint for Secrets Manager.

questions.explanation: ResourceNotFoundException in AWS Secrets Manager means the requested secret identifier cannot be resolved, often due to typos in the secret name or environment variables, or insufficient IAM permissions masking the resource.

wrongOptionNotes.A: A pending deletion KMS key causes decryption errors (KMSInvalidStateException), not a Secrets Manager ResourceNotFoundException.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Expired secrets do not throw ResourceNotFoundException; they can still be retrieved unless explicitly deleted.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Missing VPC endpoints result in connection timeouts, not a ResourceNotFoundException thrown by the SDK.

questions.question: An application deployed on AWS Elastic Beanstalk encounters persistent 502 Bad Gateway errors. The developer checks the application logs and sees that the application started successfully on port 5000, but the Nginx proxy cannot forward traffic. What configuration is likely misaligned?

options.text: The AWS Shield Advanced service has blocked the incoming requests due to suspected SQL injection.
The Application Load Balancer health check path is returning a 404 status code.
The Amazon EC2 instance IAM profile is missing permissions to read Elastic Beanstalk configuration files from S3.
The Elastic Beanstalk environment process proxy configuration is pointing to a different port than the one the application is listening on.

questions.explanation: Elastic Beanstalk container platforms utilize a reverse proxy (Nginx or Apache) to route traffic from the load balancer to the backend application. Port mismatches between the proxy configuration and the application listener result in 502 Bad Gateway errors.

wrongOptionNotes.A: AWS Shield protects against DDoS attacks; it does not generate application-level 502 Bad Gateway proxy errors.
wrongOptionNotes.B: A failing health check results in 504 Gateway Timeout or instances marked OutOfService, whereas 502 indicates a proxy communication failure to the backend port.
wrongOptionNotes.C: If the instance could not read configuration files from S3, the environment would fail to provision or launch, rather than returning running application 502 errors.

questions.question: A developer is configuring an Amazon API Gateway REST API with AWS Lambda authorizer (TOKEN type). Clients invoke the API, but receive an immediate 503 Service Unavailable response before the authorizer Lambda function is ever triggered. What is the root cause of this failure?

options.text: The Amazon API Gateway stage is not deployed with throttling limits enabled.
The Lambda authorizer returned an IAM policy document with invalid JSON syntax.
The API Gateway service lacks the necessary IAM resource-based permissions to invoke the Lambda authorizer function.
The client failed to include the Authorization header in the HTTP request.

questions.explanation: API Gateway requires explicit resource-based permissions to invoke Lambda authorizers or integration functions. Without a valid permission policy attached to the Lambda function, API Gateway cannot execute the authorizer.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Throttling limits result in 429 Too Many Requests responses, not 503 Service Unavailable.
wrongOptionNotes.B: If the authorizer executes and returns invalid JSON, API Gateway returns a 500 Internal Server Error, not 503.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Missing authorization headers typically result in a 401 Unauthorized response generated by API Gateway, not 503.

questions.question: A developer has written a Python script using Boto3 to upload confidential files to an Amazon S3 bucket. Security auditors report that files are being uploaded without server-side encryption. Which parameter must be added to the Boto3 upload_file call to enforce AES-256 encryption?

options.text: ExtraArgs={'ServerSideEncryption': 'AES256'}
Headers={'x-amz-server-side-encryption': 'AES256'}
ServerSideEncryption='aws:kms'
Encryption='AES256'

questions.explanation: The Boto3 S3 client upload methods accept an ExtraArgs parameter dictionary where developers can specify parameters like 'ServerSideEncryption': 'AES256' or 'aws:kms' to enforce encryption on uploaded objects.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Boto3 abstracts low-level HTTP headers. Passing manual HTTP headers in upload_file is incorrect; ExtraArgs must be used.
wrongOptionNotes.C: While 'aws:kms' is valid, specifying 'aws:kms' without a KMS key ID may fail or default incorrectly, and the question specifically asks for AES256 (SSE-S3).
wrongOptionNotes.D: Boto3 client and resource methods do not accept a top-level 'Encryption' keyword argument for upload functions.

questions.question: An enterprise application running on Amazon EC2 instances uses AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store to fetch configuration parameters. The application throws an AccessDeniedException when attempting to call ssm:GetParameter. The IAM role attached to the EC2 instance has a policy allowing ssm:GetParameters, but not GetParameter. How should this be resolved?

options.text: Configure the Amazon EC2 instance metadata service version 2 (IMDSv2) to allow SSM parameter caching.
Switch the parameter storage type from SecureString to String in Systems Manager Parameter Store.
Modify the application code to use the BatchGetParameter API instead of single parameter lookups.
Update the IAM policy attached to the EC2 instance role to include ssm:GetParameter for the specific parameter resource ARN.

questions.explanation: IAM policies are strictly action-based. If an application calls the ssm:GetParameter API, the calling IAM identity must possess explicit permission for ssm:GetParameter, as permissions for plural actions like GetParameters do not implicitly grant singular action access.

wrongOptionNotes.A: IMDSv2 is for instance metadata security and has no relation to Systems Manager parameter permissions.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Parameter types control encryption and pricing, not the IAM actions required to read them.
wrongOptionNotes.C: While BatchGetParameter uses GetParameters, changing code to work around IAM permission gaps is poor practice when proper least-privilege permissions should be granted.

questions.question: A developer is configuring a cross-account Amazon S3 replication rule. Objects uploaded to the source bucket in Account A are not replicating to the destination bucket in Account B, and are marked as 'Failed'. What is the most likely configuration error?

options.text: The source Amazon S3 bucket does not have versioning enabled.
The IAM replication role in Account A lacks permissions to read objects from the source bucket or write objects to the destination bucket in Account B.
The destination bucket encryption key is owned by AWS and cannot accept cross-account writes.
AWS CloudTrail is disabled in the source AWS account.

questions.explanation: S3 cross-account replication requires a robust security setup: the IAM replication role in the source account must have permissions for both source and destination buckets, and destination bucket policies must permit the replication role to put objects.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Without versioning, S3 replication cannot be enabled in the console or API, preventing configuration rather than causing runtime failure states.
wrongOptionNotes.C: SSE-S3 and SSE-KMS are both supported for cross-account S3 replication provided KMS key policies grant decrypt/encrypt access to the replication role.
wrongOptionNotes.D: CloudTrail audits API activity and is not required for data plane operations like S3 replication.

questions.question: A serverless application uses an Amazon API Gateway HTTP API integrated with an AWS Lambda function. The developer wants to ensure that requests to the API contain a custom header 'X-Custom-Token' with a specific secret value before invoking Lambda. What is the most efficient serverless approach to implement this validation?

options.text: Attach an AWS WAF WebACL to API Gateway and write a regex rule inspecting the body for the token.
Modify the backend Lambda function code to parse the event object, inspect headers, and return a 401 status if the token is missing.
Store the secret token in Amazon DynamoDB and use API Gateway VTL mapping templates to validate the request.
Configure a Lambda authorizer on the HTTP API to validate the 'X-Custom-Token' header and return an IAM policy allowing or denying access.

questions.explanation: Lambda authorizers enable API Gateway to intercept requests and delegate authentication/authorization decisions to a Lambda function, protecting backend compute resources from unauthorized requests.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Headers are not in the body, and AWS WAF can inspect headers, but Lambda authorizers are native, cost-effective, and easier for custom token validation logic in HTTP APIs.
wrongOptionNotes.B: While this works, it incurs compute costs for unauthorized invocations and wastes Lambda execution time. Security validation should occur at the gateway layer.
wrongOptionNotes.C: HTTP APIs do not support VTL mapping templates; VTL is a feature of older REST APIs.

questions.question: An application running on an Amazon EC2 instance needs to assume an IAM role in another AWS account to access a DynamoDB table. The Boto3 assume_role call fails with a ClientError indicating a security token is invalid or expired. What is the root cause?

options.text: The target IAM role's trust policy does not allow the source account's IAM role or instance profile to assume it.
The AWS SDK version installed on the EC2 instance is outdated and does not support SigV4 signing.
The EC2 instance is missing an Amazon VPC endpoint for AWS Security Token Service (STS).
The DynamoDB table item count exceeds the maximum limit for cross-account scans.

questions.explanation: Cross-account IAM role assumption via AWS STS requires two parts: the calling identity must have permission to call sts:AssumeRole, and the target IAM role must have a trust policy (resource-based policy) permitting the calling principal.

wrongOptionNotes.B: All modern AWS SDKs support SigV4 natively, and version mismatch would result in signature verification errors, not invalid token errors.
wrongOptionNotes.C: While a missing VPC endpoint could cause connection timeouts in private subnets without NAT gateways, a 'security token is invalid' error indicates an authorization or policy issue rather than a network routing failure.
wrongOptionNotes.D: DynamoDB does not restrict item counts for cross-account access; item count limits do not cause STS token errors.

questions.question: A developer is configuring an Amazon CloudFront distribution to serve static assets from a private Amazon S3 bucket. Users report getting 403 Forbidden errors when trying to load images. The S3 bucket policy blocks all public access. How should the developer secure and fix this integration?

options.text: Configure Origin Access Control (OAC) on CloudFront and update the S3 bucket policy to allow CloudFront service principal to read objects.
Configure the Application Load Balancer to proxy requests between CloudFront and S3.
Attach an IAM user policy to the CloudFront distribution configuration settings.
Enable static website hosting on the Amazon S3 bucket and make the bucket public.

questions.explanation: Amazon CloudFront Origin Access Control (OAC) is the modern recommended mechanism to secure S3 origins. It ensures buckets remain completely private while allowing authenticated requests exclusively from CloudFront distributions.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Adding an ALB between CloudFront and S3 adds unnecessary cost and architectural complexity when OAC natively solves private origin access.
wrongOptionNotes.C: CloudFront distributions cannot be assigned IAM user policies; they use service-linked roles and Origin Access controls.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Making the bucket public violates security compliance requirements and bypasses the secure private bucket mandate.

questions.question: A developer is writing an AWS Lambda function that downloads a large encrypted file from Amazon S3, decrypts it using an AWS KMS customer managed key, and processes it. The function times out after 3 minutes. CloudWatch logs show the decryption step taking excessive time. What is the most likely architectural bottleneck?

options.text: The KMS key is experiencing throttling due to exceeding cryptographic operations limits (requests per second), causing exponential backoff delays.
The S3 bucket transfer acceleration feature is disabled, causing slow file downloads.
The Lambda function memory allocation is too low, causing slow CPU-bound cryptographic calculations.
AWS Lambda does not support decrypting files larger than 1 megabyte using KMS keys.

questions.explanation: AWS KMS enforces strict limits on cryptographic requests per second. When multiple concurrent Lambda functions invoke KMS Decrypt or GenerateDataKey rapidly, throttling occurs, resulting in latency spikes and timeouts.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Transfer acceleration improves long-distance internet file transfers to S3, not KMS decryption times.
wrongOptionNotes.C: KMS decryption operations are performed off-instance by the AWS KMS service, not by the Lambda function's local CPU.
wrongOptionNotes.D: KMS generates data keys for envelope encryption or decrypts small payloads directly; large files are decrypted in streams or chunks using data keys, not by sending the entire file payload through KMS API calls.

questions.question: An AWS Lambda function needs to connect to an Amazon RDS PostgreSQL database that enforces SSL/TLS connections. The connection attempt fails with an SSL handshake exception. What is the most likely reason?

options.text: AWS Lambda prohibits outbound encrypted traffic on port 5432.
The database credentials stored in Secrets Manager were rotated, invalidating the SSL certificate.
The Lambda function code does not include or trust the AWS RDS root CA certificate bundle required to validate the database server certificate.
The Amazon RDS database security group blocks outbound traffic back to the Lambda subnet.

questions.explanation: Database connections enforcing SSL/TLS require client applications to trust the server's certificate. Because AWS RDS uses certificates signed by specific internal CAs, database client code must bundle and reference the corresponding AWS RDS root CA certificate.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Lambda has no network port restrictions on outbound traffic; port 5432 is standard for PostgreSQL.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Rotating database passwords changes credentials, not the underlying SSL/TLS certificate authority used for cryptographic verification.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Security groups in AWS are stateful. Return traffic for established connections is automatically allowed regardless of outbound rules.

questions.question: A developer is configuring a secure AWS Lambda function that must process incoming messages from an Amazon SQS queue. The SQS queue is encrypted using a custom AWS KMS customer managed key (CMK). When testing the Lambda function, messages are failing to process, and logs show an AccessDeniedException when the function attempts to read from the queue. What must the developer configure to resolve this issue?

options.text: Enable SQS server-side encryption using the default AWS managed key (aws/sqs) instead of a custom KMS key.
Configure the Amazon SQS queue policy to allow public read access for all encrypted messages.
Attach an Amazon SQS FullAccess policy directly to the AWS Lambda function's resource-based policy.
Add the Lambda execution role's ARN to the KMS key's policy as a key user, and grant the execution role decrypt permissions for the SQS queue's KMS key.

questions.explanation: To allow an AWS Lambda function to consume messages from an encrypted Amazon SQS queue using a custom KMS key, the Lambda execution role needs both permissions to poll the queue (sqs:ReceiveMessage, sqs:DeleteMessage, sqs:GetQueueAttributes) and permissions to decrypt the payload via the KMS key (kms:Decrypt) specified in the key policy or IAM policy.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Switching to an AWS managed key may bypass the custom key issue, but it violates the compliance requirement of using a customer managed key.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Making an SQS queue publicly accessible violates baseline cloud security and compliance standards.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Lambda functions do not use resource-based policies for outbound access to SQS; they use execution IAM roles, and FullAccess violates least privilege.

questions.question: An enterprise developer needs to ensure that all newly created Amazon S3 buckets across multiple AWS accounts in an AWS Organization automatically enforce bucket ownership settings to block public ACLs. Which AWS feature should the developer implement to enforce this governance requirement?

options.text: AWS IAM permissions boundaries applied to every user and role within each account.
AWS CloudTrail log analysis coupled with an automated Amazon EventBridge rule to delete public buckets.
AWS Organizations Service Control Policies (SCPs) combined with S3 Block Public Access at the bucket level.
An AWS Organizations Service Control Policy (SCP) that restricts the creation of S3 buckets unless S3 Block Public Access is enabled or enforced.

questions.explanation: AWS Organizations Service Control Policies (SCPs) allow administrators to centrally control permissions across multiple AWS accounts. By writing an SCP that denies S3 operations unless specific security conditions (like S3 Block Public Access) are met, enterprises can enforce mandatory compliance guardrails.

wrongOptionNotes.A: IAM permissions boundaries limit maximum permissions, but they do not specifically enforce S3 bucket ownership settings or block public ACLs automatically.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Reactive remediation via EventBridge leaves a window of vulnerability during which a public bucket can be exploited before deletion.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Relying on manual S3 Block Public Access configuration per bucket does not guarantee automated enforcement across all accounts.

questions.question: A developer is writing code for an AWS Lambda function that needs to call external third-party APIs over the internet. The Lambda function must be deployed inside a private VPC subnet for database access compliance, but it still requires secure outbound internet access without exposing its private IP address inbound. Which architecture satisfies these requirements?

options.text: Assign a public IPv4 address directly to the ENI created by the Lambda function inside the private subnet.
Deploy the Lambda function in a private subnet, attach an Internet Gateway to the VPC, and add a default route pointing to the Internet Gateway.
Deploy the Lambda function in a private subnet and route outbound internet traffic through a NAT Gateway located in a public subnet.
Configure an Amazon VPC endpoint of type Interface for the third-party API domain.

questions.explanation: When an AWS Lambda function requires both VPC resource access and outbound internet access, it must be placed in a private subnet. Outbound internet traffic is routed through a NAT Gateway located in a public subnet, enabling secure egress while maintaining isolation from inbound traffic.

wrongOptionNotes.A: AWS Lambda functions running inside a VPC do not support assigning public IP addresses to their elastic network interfaces (ENIs).
wrongOptionNotes.B: Private subnets cannot directly route traffic through an Internet Gateway; they require a NAT Gateway or NAT instance.
wrongOptionNotes.D: VPC Interface endpoints are designed for AWS services and supported third-party services integrated with PrivateLink, not arbitrary external public APIs.

questions.question: A developer needs to configure least-privilege access for an AWS Lambda function that updates specific items in an Amazon DynamoDB table named UserSession. The function should only be allowed to modify the 'status' and 'lastLogin' attributes of items where the partition key matches the user ID. Which IAM policy statement adheres best to the principle of least privilege?

options.text: An IAM policy allowing dynamodb:UpdateItem on the UserSession table ARN with a condition limiting the update expression to specific attributes.
An IAM policy allowing dynamodb:PutItem and dynamodb:GetItem on all DynamoDB tables in the account.
An IAM policy granting administrator access if the Lambda execution role originates from a trusted VPC.
An IAM policy allowing dynamodb:* on the UserSession table resource.

questions.explanation: Least privilege requires restricting permissions to only the necessary actions on specific resources. For DynamoDB, using `UpdateItem` with granular condition keys and attribute constraints prevents unauthorized modifications to sensitive table columns.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Granting access to all DynamoDB tables in the account exposes unrelated data stores to potential compromise.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Administrator access should never be granted based solely on network origin, as it bypasses resource- and action-level least privilege controls.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Using dynamodb:* grants excessive administrative and read/write privileges, violating the principle of least privilege.

questions.question: An application running on an Amazon EC2 instance needs to securely retrieve sensitive API keys stored in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. The parameter value is encrypted using a custom AWS KMS customer managed key (CMK). Which set of permissions must be granted to the EC2 instance profile for successful retrieval?

options.text: ec2:DescribeInstances and s3:GetObject permissions on the shared configuration bucket.
ssm:PutParameter and kms:Encrypt permissions assigned to the EC2 instance profile IAM role.
ssm:GetParameter and kms:Decrypt permissions assigned to the EC2 instance profile IAM role.
sts:AssumeRole permissions on the AWS Systems Manager service principal.

questions.explanation: Retrieving encrypted parameters (SecureString) from Systems Manager Parameter Store requires both Parameter Store read permissions (`ssm:GetParameter` or `ssm:GetParameters`) and KMS decryption permissions (`kms:Decrypt`) on the specific key protecting the parameter.

wrongOptionNotes.A: EC2 description permissions and S3 object permissions are unrelated to retrieving secure configuration parameters from Systems Manager.
wrongOptionNotes.B: PutParameter and Encrypt are write and encryption operations, whereas the application only needs read and decryption capabilities.
wrongOptionNotes.D: EC2 instance profiles authenticate directly using instance metadata; they do not assume the SSM service principal to read parameters.

questions.question: A developer is building a microservice that exposes sensitive financial data. The service runs on AWS Lambda and is invoked via an Amazon API Gateway REST API. The security team mandates that all incoming requests must be authenticated using JSON Web Tokens (JWT) issued by an enterprise identity provider, and authorization decisions must be validated at the API Gateway layer before reaching Lambda. Which configuration meets this requirement with minimal custom code?

options.text: Attach an AWS WAF WebACL to API Gateway and configure a regex match rule to inspect JWT claims.
Write a custom AWS Lambda function to inspect the HTTP authorization header and decode the JWT manually inside the backend Lambda code.
Configure an Amazon Cognito user pool authorizer or a JWT authorizer directly on the API Gateway route.
Configure an Amazon S3 bucket policy to intercept API Gateway HTTP requests and validate token claims.

questions.explanation: Using native API Gateway JWT authorizers offloads authentication and token verification (such as signature verification and expiration checking) to the API Gateway edge, preventing unauthorized requests from hitting backend Lambda functions.

wrongOptionNotes.A: AWS WAF inspects web traffic patterns and SQL injections, but it is not designed to cryptographic signature validation and claims parsing for JWTs.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Validating tokens inside the backend Lambda requires custom code and allows unauthenticated requests to consume backend compute resources before rejection.
wrongOptionNotes.D: S3 bucket policies govern access to S3 objects, not API Gateway HTTP requests or JWT token validation.

questions.question: A developer is managing an Amazon S3 bucket that receives sensitive compliance reports from external partners. To comply with regulatory standards, the developer must ensure that no object in the bucket can be deleted or overwritten by any user, including the root account user, for a retention period of 365 days. Which S3 feature should be configured?

options.text: S3 Object Lock in Compliance mode set to a retention period of 365 days.
S3 Lifecycle Configuration rules transitioning objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 1 day.
S3 Bucket Policies denying all s3:DeleteObject actions without an MFA delete condition.
S3 Object Lock in Governance mode set to a retention period of 365 days.

questions.explanation: S3 Object Lock in Compliance mode ensures WORM (Write Once, Read Many) storage. When enabled, no user—including the account root user—can overwrite or delete protected objects until the retention period expires.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Lifecycle policies manage storage classes and expiration, but they do not enforce immutability or prevent deletion.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Bucket policies can be modified or deleted by administrators with appropriate permissions, failing to provide immutable compliance protection.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Governance mode allows users with specific IAM permissions (such as bypass governance) to override retention settings, which violates strict compliance requirements.

questions.question: A financial application running on Amazon EC2 needs to connect to an Amazon RDS MySQL database. Security policies dictate that database credentials must be rotated automatically every 30 days without application downtime, and application code must never hardcode or statically store credentials. What is the AWS-recommended architecture to achieve this?

options.text: Store credentials in an encrypted text file on an Amazon EBS volume attached to the EC2 instance, and use a cron job to update the file monthly.
Store credentials in AWS Secrets Manager and configure automatic rotation using an AWS Lambda rotation function.
Store database credentials as plain text tags on the EC2 instance and RDS database resources.
Hardcode credentials inside AWS CloudFormation templates and update the template parameters every 30 days.

questions.explanation: AWS Secrets Manager provides built-in secret rotation capabilities backed by AWS Lambda. Applications query Secrets Manager at runtime to fetch current credentials, eliminating hardcoded secrets and supporting seamless automatic rotation.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Storing passwords in flat files on EBS volumes is insecure and risks credential exposure if the volume snapshot is shared or compromised.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Resource tags are visible in plain text to anyone with read access to AWS resource metadata, making them unsuitable for secrets storage.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Hardcoding credentials in templates exposes secrets in plain text within version control and CloudFormation state histories.

questions.question: An AWS Lambda function needs to assume an IAM role in another AWS account to access an encrypted Amazon S3 bucket. The trust policy of the cross-account role is configured correctly, but calls to S3 fail with an access denied error. What additional configuration is required to allow successful cross-account access?

options.text: Enable public read access on the S3 bucket to bypass cross-account authentication checks.
The resource-based bucket policy on the target S3 bucket in the second account must explicitly allow the assumed IAM role principal.
The Lambda function must be deployed inside a VPC peering connection spanning both AWS accounts.
The AWS Lambda function execution timeout must be increased to at least 15 minutes to handle cross-account handshake overhead.

questions.explanation: Cross-account access in AWS requires evaluation of both the IAM permissions (identity-based policy or assumed role) and the resource-based policy. For Amazon S3, the destination bucket policy must explicitly permit actions for the external IAM role or account.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Opening S3 buckets to public read access introduces severe security risks and is a violation of security hardening best practices.
wrongOptionNotes.C: IAM and S3 access are managed via API authorization policies, not VPC peering connections.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Timeout settings affect execution duration limits, not cryptographic or IAM authorization failures.

questions.question: A developer is configuring an Amazon CloudFront distribution to serve private media files stored in an Amazon S3 bucket. To ensure users cannot bypass CloudFront and access the S3 bucket directly via public URLs, what is the most secure configuration to implement?

options.text: Use Origin Access Control (OAC) to restrict access to the S3 bucket so that only the specified CloudFront distribution can read objects.
Store the S3 bucket name in a public DNS TXT record so CloudFront can validate authorized requests.
Grant CloudFront root account credentials to the S3 bucket via cross-account IAM trust relationships.
Configure an S3 bucket policy allowing public read access for all IP addresses except those originating from CloudFront.

questions.explanation: Amazon CloudFront Origin Access Control (OAC) allows developers to completely lock down S3 buckets by blocking public access while permitting CloudFront to securely access objects using SigV4 signed requests.

wrongOptionNotes.B: DNS TXT records have no role in securing S3 origin access or authenticating CloudFront requests.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Sharing account root credentials is a severe security violation and is not supported for CloudFront-S3 integration.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Relying on IP blacklisting or public bucket policies leaves the bucket vulnerable to direct unauthorized downloads.

questions.question: A developer is writing an AWS CloudFormation template that provisions an IAM role for an Amazon ECS task. Security standards dictate that no inline policies should be used; all permissions must be attached via managed policies. Furthermore, the role must not be able to assume any higher privilege than necessary. Which CloudFormation snippet configuration implements this correctly?

options.text: Use an AWS::IAM::InstanceProfile resource for ECS tasks running on Fargate.
Define an AWS::IAM::Role resource with an inline Policies property granting AdministratorAccess.
Attach AWS managed policies directly to the Amazon ECS cluster resource instead of an IAM role.
Define an AWS::IAM::Role resource with ManagedPolicyArns pointing to specific AWS or customer managed policies, omitting the Policies property entirely.

questions.explanation: In AWS CloudFormation, `AWS::IAM::Role` resources can be provisioned using `ManagedPolicyArns` to attach managed policies cleanly without embedding inline policies, maintaining compliance with security baselines.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Instance profiles are used exclusively for EC2 instances, whereas ECS Fargate tasks utilize task execution roles and task roles directly.
wrongOptionNotes.B: AdministratorAccess violates the principle of least privilege, and the scenario explicitly prohibits inline policies.
wrongOptionNotes.C: ECS clusters do not accept IAM policies directly; task execution roles and task roles are assigned at the task definition level.

questions.question: A company requires that all data stored in Amazon EBS volumes attached to Amazon EC2 instances must be encrypted at rest. A developer is launching a new EC2 instance via an AWS CloudFormation template. How should the developer configure the EBS volume to ensure mandatory encryption at rest?

options.text: Enable Amazon S3 server-side encryption on the EC2 instance configuration settings.
Attach an IAM policy to the EC2 instance requiring encryption keys during runtime writes.
Configure the BlockDeviceMappings property in the AWS::EC2::Instance resource with Encrypted set to true.
Rely on the default EC2 operating system file system to encrypt files automatically after the instance boots.

questions.explanation: Amazon EBS volume encryption can be enforced when launching EC2 instances or creating volumes via CloudFormation by setting `Encrypted: true` in the block device mapping, ensuring all data at rest is encrypted using KMS keys.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Amazon S3 server-side encryption applies to object storage in S3 buckets, not EBS block storage volumes attached to EC2.
wrongOptionNotes.B: EBS volume encryption at rest must be configured at the block storage level during volume provisioning, not via runtime IAM policies.
wrongOptionNotes.D: OS-level encryption does not encrypt the underlying EBS block storage volumes at rest from an infrastructure perspective.

questions.question: An application running on an Amazon EC2 instance needs to securely sign outgoing requests to an AWS service using Signature Version 4. The developer wants to avoid hardcoding AWS credentials or storing long-term IAM user access keys on the instance file system. What is the AWS best-practice approach?

options.text: Attach an IAM role to the Amazon EC2 instance profile, allowing the AWS SDK to automatically retrieve and manage temporary security credentials.
Configure a public IAM user with programmatic access and share the keys across all EC2 instances in the fleet.
Hardcode AWS credentials inside the application source code configuration file with read-only file permissions.
Store AWS IAM user access keys and secret keys in an environment variable file readable only by the root user.

questions.explanation: To adhere to AWS security best practices, applications running on EC2 should always use IAM roles attached via instance profiles. AWS SDKs automatically handle obtaining, using, and refreshing temporary credentials via the Instance Metadata Service (IMDS).

wrongOptionNotes.B: Sharing long-term user credentials across multiple instances violates the principle of least privilege and auditability.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Hardcoding credentials in source code violates security best practices and exposes secrets if code repositories are leaked.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Storing long-term access keys on instances introduces significant security risks if the instance is compromised.

questions.question: A developer is configuring an AWS CloudTrail trail to record all management events across an entire AWS Organization. Security compliance mandates that the CloudTrail log files stored in an Amazon S3 bucket must be validated to ensure they have not been modified or tampered with after delivery. Which CloudTrail feature should the developer enable?

options.text: Amazon S3 Versioning combined with Cross-Region Replication
Amazon CloudWatch Logs metric filters scanning for unauthorized API calls
CloudTrail Log File Integrity Validation
AWS IAM Access Analyzer monitoring on the CloudTrail S3 bucket policy

questions.explanation: CloudTrail log file integrity validation computes a digital signature for every log file delivered to S3. Developers can use these hashes to cryptographically prove that the log files were unaltered since creation.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Versioning and replication protect against accidental deletion or regional outages, but they do not provide cryptographic proof of log integrity against tampering.
wrongOptionNotes.B: CloudWatch metric filters monitor log content for specific patterns, but they do not validate log file cryptographic integrity.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Access Analyzer checks for unintended public or cross-account access, not file modification or log tampering.

questions.question: A developer is writing a backend Node.js application that runs inside an Amazon ECS container on AWS Fargate. The application needs to connect to an Amazon Aurora database. Security policies require that database passwords must never be visible in plaintext in the ECS task definition or environment variables. How should the developer supply the database password to the container securely?

options.text: Store the database password in an unencrypted Amazon S3 text file and have the container download it on startup using public HTTP URLs.
Pass the password as a plaintext string in the environment section of the ECS task definition container definitions.
Reference the secret stored in AWS Secrets Manager or Systems Manager Parameter Store using the secrets property in the ECS task definition container definition.
Hardcode the password in a configuration JSON file bundled inside the Docker image before pushing to Amazon ECR.

questions.explanation: Amazon ECS task definitions allow developers to securely inject sensitive data into containers using the `secrets` configuration block, referencing keys stored securely in AWS Secrets Manager or Systems Manager Parameter Store.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Storing passwords in unencrypted S3 files accessed via public URLs is insecure and violates basic data protection standards.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Putting passwords in task definition environment variables exposes them in plaintext via the AWS Management Console and API calls.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Embedding secrets inside Docker images exposes them to anyone with pull access to the ECR repository.

questions.question: A high-throughput financial transaction processing application running on AWS Lambda needs to fetch database credentials frequently. To minimize latency and control costs under strict budget constraints, which design pattern should the developer implement?

options.text: Retrieve the credentials from AWS Secrets Manager once outside the handler function during cold start and cache them globally in execution environment memory.
Store the plaintext database credentials directly in the Lambda environment variables with encryption helpers enabled.
Call AWS Secrets Manager directly inside the function handler on every invocation to ensure the latest credentials are always used.
Provision an Amazon ElastiCache cluster to centrally store and serve database credentials to all concurrent Lambda instances.

questions.explanation: For serverless applications under high throughput and strict cost constraints, caching secrets outside the Lambda handler function leverages execution environment reuse. This pattern drastically reduces both API request costs to Secrets Manager and function execution latency.

wrongOptionNotes.B: While environment variables are cached, storing unencrypted or loosely managed plaintext credentials violates security best practices, even with encryption helpers.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Calling Secrets Manager on every invocation introduces significant API latency and incurs high costs due to API call pricing at scale.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Introducing ElastiCache adds unnecessary infrastructure costs and operational complexity for simply caching static or infrequently rotated database credentials.

questions.question: An enterprise application hosted on Amazon EC2 needs to download large configuration files from a private Amazon S3 bucket. Due to strict data transfer budget limits, the developer must prevent high NAT Gateway data processing fees. How should the developer architect this access?

options.text: Attach a public IP address directly to the private EC2 instance so it can access S3 over the internet.
Configure an AWS PrivateLink Gateway VPC Endpoint for Amazon S3 in the VPC and route traffic through it.
Deploy a custom proxy server on an EC2 instance in a public subnet to forward requests to Amazon S3.
Route all S3 traffic through a NAT Gateway attached to a public subnet in the VPC.

questions.explanation: Gateway VPC Endpoints for Amazon S3 provide a cost-effective and secure way to connect VPC instances to S3 without traversing NAT Gateways or the public internet, eliminating hourly and data-processing charges associated with NAT.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Exposing internal private instances to the public internet via public IP addresses introduces severe security vulnerabilities.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Managing a custom proxy server introduces unnecessary maintenance overhead, single points of failure, and additional compute costs.
wrongOptionNotes.D: NAT Gateways process all outbound traffic and incur significant per-gigabyte data processing fees, violating the budget constraint.

questions.question: A developer is configuring an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of an Amazon S3 bucket. To optimize performance and reduce origin fetch costs, the developer needs to cache static content effectively while ensuring unauthorized users cannot access restricted objects. Which approach achieves this securely and cost-effectively?

options.text: Write a custom Lambda@Edge viewer-request function to authenticate every incoming request against a DynamoDB table before hitting cache.
Use CloudFront signed URLs combined with Origin Access Control (OAC) to restrict direct S3 access and securely serve cached content.
Disable caching on the CloudFront distribution to force all requests to validate against the S3 origin.
Make all objects in the S3 bucket public so CloudFront can fetch them without authentication overhead.

questions.explanation: CloudFront Origin Access Control (OAC) protects S3 buckets by restricting access exclusively to the specified CloudFront distribution, allowing safe caching of private assets without exposing the origin bucket.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Executing a database lookup on every viewer request at the edge incurs massive Lambda@Edge execution costs and increases latency.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Disabling caching defeats the primary purpose of CloudFront, spiking origin load and increasing data transfer costs.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Making S3 objects public compromises security, exposing sensitive files directly to the public internet.

questions.question: An AWS Lambda function processing sensitive webhook payloads needs to decrypt incoming data encrypted with an AWS KMS customer managed key (CMK). To minimize KMS API invocation costs under high message volume, what is the best practice?

options.text: Use AWS Encryption SDK to encrypt data client-side with a data key cache, reducing direct KMS API calls during high-throughput processing.
Disable KMS encryption and store payloads in plaintext to eliminate performance overhead and API costs entirely.
Migrate the processing logic to an unmanaged EC2 instance and handle decryption locally using OpenSSL.
Call the KMS Decrypt API for every single incoming webhook payload individually.

questions.explanation: Using client-side caching via libraries like the AWS Encryption SDK allows applications to perform cryptographic operations locally for a defined time or size limit, minimizing costly calls to AWS KMS.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Storing sensitive payloads in plaintext violates core security compliance and data protection standards.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Moving away from serverless introduces infrastructure management overhead and fails to solve the KMS cost architectural pattern.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Invoking KMS Decrypt for every single message at high volume incurs steep API call charges and risks throttling.
