Add the ForceDelete: true property to the AWS::S3::Bucket resource definition properties.

questions.explanation: Amazon S3 buckets must be empty before CloudFormation can delete them. The standard remediation for automated stack deletion of buckets containing application data is implementing an AWS Lambda-backed custom resource that catches stack deletion events and empties the S3 bucket.

wrongOptionNotes.B: S3 lifecycle rules execute asynchronously and are not instantaneous, meaning a stack deletion attempt could still encounter objects before lifecycle expiration completes.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Retain tells CloudFormation to skip deleting the resource when the stack is deleted, leaving the bucket orphan-managed, but it does not solve cleanup if standard deletion is attempted on a non-empty bucket.
wrongOptionNotes.D: There is no ForceDelete property in the AWS::S3::Bucket resource specification in CloudFormation.

questions.question: A developer is configuring an AWS CodePipeline pipeline that builds a React single-page application and deploys the static build artifacts to an Amazon S3 bucket configured for static website hosting. After deployment, users report that navigating directly to sub-routes results in 404 Not Found errors from Amazon S3, although the root URL loads correctly. What is the root cause and remediation?

options.text: The CodeBuild buildspec is omitting the public-read canned ACL when uploading files to S3 via the aws s3 sync command.

Amazon S3 static website hosting does not natively handle client-side routing; the developer must configure custom error document redirection rules in S3 to redirect all 404 errors to index.html with a 200 status code.
The S3 bucket policy is missing a public Read permission statement forGetObject actions.
The CodePipeline S3 deployment action must be configured with cache-control headers set to no-cache.

questions.explanation: Single-page applications (SPAs) handled by client-side JavaScript routers require server-side redirection support. Because Amazon S3 static website hosting looks for physical objects corresponding to requested URIs, routing rules must be configured in S3 to redirect 404 errors back to the root index.html file.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Canned ACLs control access permissions, not client-side URL routing behavior for single-page applications.
wrongOptionNotes.C: If the bucket policy lacked GetObject permissions, the root URL would also return 404 or 403 errors, rather than only sub-routes failing.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Cache-control headers manage browser caching behavior, not HTTP 404 errors returned for non-existent S3 object keys.

questions.question: A developer is deploying a microservice to an Amazon ECS cluster using AWS CodeDeploy with a Blue/Green deployment strategy. The developer notices that after the new deployment succeeds, old Amazon ECS task sets are immediately terminated without allowing any time for operational observation or alarm evaluation. How should the developer configure a stabilization window?

options.text: Add a CloudWatch alarm to the deployment group and set the evaluation periods to 10 minutes.
Modify the AWS::ECS::Service resource in CloudFormation to set MaximumPercent to 200 and MinimumHealthyPercent to 100.
Configure the deployment configuration (e.g., CodeDeployDefault.ECSAllAtOnce or a custom deployment config) to include a termination wait time using the BlueGreenDeploymentConfiguration settings.
Set the HealthCheckGracePeriodSeconds parameter in the ECS service definition to 600 seconds.

questions.explanation: AWS CodeDeploy provides built-in control over when old tasks are terminated following a successful deployment via the termination wait time configuration. This allows operators time to observe application metrics before the old task set is decommissioned.

wrongOptionNotes.A: CloudWatch alarms monitor health metrics during deployment, but they do not control the automatic termination delay window for old task sets once deployment completes.
wrongOptionNotes.B: These parameters control rolling update mechanics in native ECS services, not CodeDeploy Blue/Green deployment task set lifecycle termination delays.
wrongOptionNotes.D: HealthCheckGracePeriodSeconds applies to newly started tasks during container initialization to prevent premature ELB health check failures, not post-deployment task retention.

questions.question: A developer is writing an AWS CloudFormation template that deploys an application stack. The template needs to provision different resource configurations depending on whether the target environment is 'staging' or 'production'. The developer wants to select the appropriate instance type cleanly without duplicating resource blocks. Which CloudFormation feature should be used?

options.text: CloudFormation StackSets with automatic parameter injection.
CloudFormation Mappings combined with the Fn::FindInMap intrinsic function.
The Fn::ImportValue intrinsic function referencing outputs from a shared networking stack.
AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store parameters resolved at runtime using Dynamic References ({{resolve:ssm}}).

questions.explanation: CloudFormation Mappings act as a conditional lookup table. By defining a Mapping section in the template and querying it with Fn::FindInMap based on a Parameter representing the environment, developers can cleanly assign environment-specific property values.

wrongOptionNotes.A: StackSets are used to deploy stacks across multiple accounts and regions concurrently, not for environment-specific parameter resolution within a single template.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Fn::ImportValue imports exported outputs from other active stacks, which is used for cross-stack references rather than environment-based configuration selection.
wrongOptionNotes.D: While dynamic references can fetch parameters from SSM, CloudFormation Mappings are the idiomatic declarative mechanism for embedding environment-specific configuration tables directly within a template.

questions.question: A developer is configuring an AWS CodeBuild project that runs integration tests requiring access to an external third-party API. The API credentials are confidential and must not be stored in plain text within the buildspec file or source repository. What is the most secure and recommended way to provide these credentials to CodeBuild?

options.text: Save the credentials in an Amazon S3 bucket with public read access disabled and download them using the AWS CLI during the pre_build phase.

Store the credentials securely in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store (SecureString) or AWS Secrets Manager, and reference them directly in the CodeBuild project environment configuration or buildspec.
Store the credentials as secure plaintext parameters in the CodeBuild project environment variables section via the AWS Management Console.
Encrypt the credentials with a local GPG key and commit the encrypted file to the Git repository alongside a decryption script running during build initialization.

questions.explanation: AWS CodeBuild supports secure integration with AWS Secrets Manager and Systems Manager Parameter Store. Referencing secrets directly in the project configuration ensures that sensitive credentials are securely injected into the build container environment at runtime.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Downloading secrets from S3 requires hardcoding bucket references and credentials for the download action, failing secure secret management best practices.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Standard environment variables entered in plaintext or standard UI fields are visible in console views and can be extracted if build logs inadvertently print environment variables.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Committing encrypted secrets and managing decryption keys inside build pipelines introduces unnecessary key management overhead and security risks.

questions.question: A developer has configured an AWS CodePipeline pipeline with multiple actions in a single stage. When the pipeline executes, the developer notices that the actions within that single stage execute sequentially rather than concurrently. How can the developer modify the stage configuration to ensure concurrent execution?

options.text: Set the concurrency attribute to parallel in the pipeline JSON structure under the stage definition block.
Upgrade the pipeline type from V1 to V2, which introduces multi-threaded stage processing capabilities.
By default, actions within a single stage execute sequentially. To run actions concurrently, the developer must place them into separate, parallel stages in the pipeline.
Ensure that the actions within the stage do not declare input artifacts that depend on the output artifacts of preceding actions within the exact same stage.

questions.explanation: In AWS CodePipeline, actions within the same stage execute concurrently by default, unless an action specifies an input artifact that is produced by a preceding action in that same stage. Removing artifact dependencies between independent actions enables parallel execution.

wrongOptionNotes.A: There is no concurrency attribute in stage definitions; parallel execution is governed implicitly by artifact dependency flow.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Pipeline V2 introduces features like triggers and execution modes, but action concurrency within a stage is fundamentally determined by artifact passing dependencies.
wrongOptionNotes.C: CodePipeline actually supports parallel action execution within the same stage if actions do not share input/output artifact dependencies.

questions.question: A developer is troubleshooting an AWS Elastic Beanstalk application running on a fleet of Amazon EC2 instances. The application writes log files to a custom local directory (/var/log/myapp), but these logs do not appear in the default bundle downloaded via the Elastic Beanstalk console ('Request Logs'). How should the developer configure Elastic Beanstalk to bundle and stream these custom logs?

options.text: Modify the Auto Scaling launch template user data script to run an rsync cron job copying logs to /var/log/eb-engine.log.

Create a configuration file (e.g., .ebextensions/01_custom_logs.config) containing a files block that places a configuration file in /opt/elasticbeanstalk/tasks/bundlelogs.d/ to include the custom directory path.
Add a configuration file (.config) in the .ebextensions directory that uses the files and commands keys to install an Amazon CloudWatch Agent configuration streaming the directory.
Update the Elastic Beanstalk environment service role IAM policy to include s3:PutObject permissions for the custom log path.

questions.explanation: AWS Elastic Beanstalk allows developers to customize log bundling by placing configuration files in .ebextensions that define custom log streaming rules. By instructing the Beanstalk log-gathering daemon about additional application log paths, developers ensure custom logs are included in standard log retrieval requests.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Writing cron jobs to overwrite internal engine logs is an anti-pattern that disrupts Elastic Beanstalk's platform monitoring agent.
wrongOptionNotes.C: While CloudWatch streaming is valid, Elastic Beanstalk has a built-in log streaming mechanism specifically designed for the 'Request Logs' bundle feature.
wrongOptionNotes.D: IAM permissions govern authorization to AWS APIs, not local log file discovery and bundling behavior on EC2 instances.

questions.question: A developer has configured an AWS CodePipeline pipeline that deploys a microservice to AWS Lambda. After merging a new version of the code, the pipeline execution succeeds, but users report that the application behavior has not changed. Investigations show that the Lambda function configuration points to the correct function name, but the runtime environment is executing stale code. What is the most likely root cause and solution?

options.text: The CodeDeploy deployment group associated with the pipeline is deploying to the wrong alias; the developer must update the AppSpec file to target the correct Lambda function alias or version.
AWS CodePipeline requires a manual approval action before promoting new code to production Lambda functions, which stalled the traffic shift.
The Lambda function deployment package exceeded the size limit for direct updates, requiring the developer to upload the artifact to Amazon S3 first.
Amazon API Gateway caches the Lambda function responses for 24 hours by default, so the developer must manually flush the stage cache in API Gateway.

questions.explanation: In AWS Lambda deployments managed by AWS CodeDeploy, updates must correctly manage function versions and aliases. If the deployment updates only the unpublished version ($LATEST) while API consumers invoke a specific production alias, the changes will not be visible to users until the alias is updated to point to the new version.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Manual approval stops pipeline execution entirely; if the pipeline reported success, no approval stage was pending.
wrongOptionNotes.C: If a deployment package exceeds direct upload limits, the deployment fails with an error rather than reporting a false success while running stale code.
wrongOptionNotes.D: While API Gateway caching can cause stale responses, it does not explain why the underlying Lambda runtime environment itself runs stale code logic if code was updated directly. The issue stems from versioning and alias routing.

questions.question: A developer is troubleshooting an AWS Elastic Beanstalk application that fails to deploy a new version. The environment events log shows an error indicating that the application failed to start because required environment variables defined in the configuration files were missing. Where should the developer inspect and configure these environment variables to resolve the deployment failure permanently?

options.text: Define the environment variables under the option settings in the Elastic Beanstalk console configuration or within an .ebextensions configuration file using the aws:elasticbeanstalk:application:environment namespace.
Configure the variables as parameters inside AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store and attach the AmazonSSMReadOnlyAccess policy to the Auto Scaling group launch template.
Modify the AWS CloudFormation template generated by Elastic Beanstalk to inject the variables directly into the Amazon EC2 user data script.
Store the variables inside an Amazon S3 bucket named elasticbeanstalk-environment-variables and grant the instance profile read access.

questions.explanation: AWS Elastic Beanstalk provides a built-in configuration mechanism for environment variables using the aws:elasticbeanstalk:application:environment namespace. Developers can define these in .ebextensions files or via the console/CLI to ensure they are available to the application upon startup.

wrongOptionNotes.B: While Parameter Store can store secrets, Elastic Beanstalk has a native environment property mechanism that must be used for standard application configuration.
wrongOptionNotes.C: While user data can run scripts, modifying underlying generated CloudFormation templates directly is discouraged and overridden during environment updates.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Elastic Beanstalk does not automatically read environment variables from a conventionally named S3 bucket.

questions.question: A developer is implementing a blue/green deployment for an Amazon ECS service using AWS CodeDeploy with the CodeDeployDefault.ECSAllAtOnce configuration. During the deployment, the new task definition is instantiated, but the deployment immediately fails before shifting traffic because health checks on the new containers timeout. What is the most appropriate troubleshooting step?

options.text: Increase the CodeDeploy deployment lifecycle hook timeout to 2 hours to allow tasks more time to initialize.
Inspect the Amazon ECS task container logs in Amazon CloudWatch Logs to identify application startup errors or misconfigured health check paths.
Switch the deployment configuration to CodeDeployDefault.ECSCanary10Percent10Minutes to give instances more time to spin up.
Modify the Application Load Balancer listener rule to bypass health checks for blue/green deployments.

questions.explanation: When ECS tasks fail health checks during a CodeDeploy deployment, developers must check Amazon CloudWatch Logs for the container tasks to identify runtime errors, missing environment variables, or incorrect health check endpoints.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Increasing lifecycle hook timeouts does not fix the underlying application startup failure or container health check misconfigurations.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Changing the traffic shifting strategy does not resolve underlying application crashes or health check failures.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Health checks cannot and should not be bypassed, as they ensure traffic is only routed to healthy container instances.

questions.question: A developer is writing an AWS CloudFormation template that deploys an AWS Lambda function and an Amazon API Gateway REST API. The developer needs to ensure that whenever the Lambda function code updates, the API Gateway deployment automatically updates to serve the new version without requiring manual intervention in the console. Which architectural pattern should the developer implement in CloudFormation?

options.text: Add a DependsOn attribute to the API Gateway Deployment resource referencing a custom AWS::CloudFormation::Macro that recalculates function hashes.

Include a hash of the Lambda function source code or deployment archive in the description or logical ID suffix of the AWS::ApiGateway::Deployment resource so that changes force a new deployment resource.
Configure the AWS::ApiGateway::Stage resource with an AutoDeploy property set to true.
Configure an AWS Lambda permission resource with an event source mapping to automatically redeploy the API Gateway stage.

questions.explanation: CloudFormation treats API Gateway deployments as static resources unless a property changes. By incorporating a hash of the Lambda function's source code or S3 object version into the Deployment resource (such as in its description or logical ID), any change to the code modifies the deployment resource and triggers a fresh API deployment.

wrongOptionNotes.A: CloudFormation macros manipulate templates during creation, but do not automatically trigger API Gateway deployments when code hashes change without specific resource changes.
wrongOptionNotes.C: The AutoDeploy property is available for API Gateway HTTP APIs, but REST APIs managed via CloudFormation require explicit Deployment resources.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Event source mappings are used for services like DynamoDB and Kinesis, not for managing API Gateway stage deployments.

questions.question: A developer is configuring an AWS CodeBuild project that builds a Docker container image and pushes it to Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR). The buildspec.yml file executes successfully, but the build fails during the docker push phase with an 'AccessDeniedException' or 'no basic auth credentials' error. What is the most likely cause of this failure?

options.text: The Docker container image tag exceeds the 128-character limit imposed by Amazon ECR.
The Amazon ECR repository policy blocks public access from outside the VPC.
The CodeBuild service role lacks permissions to perform Amazon ECR authorization and push actions, or the buildspec did not execute 'aws ecr get-login-password'.
Docker daemon is not running inside the CodeBuild managed container environment.

questions.explanation: Pushing images to Amazon ECR from AWS CodeBuild requires two components: proper IAM permissions attached to the CodeBuild service role for ECR actions, and explicit authentication commands (such as running `aws ecr get-login-password`) inside the buildspec before executing `docker push`.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Exceeding tag limits results in a validation exception rather than an authentication or authorization failure.
wrongOptionNotes.B: CodeBuild communicates with ECR via AWS API endpoints over HTTPS, not public internet routing that would be restricted by typical public-blocking bucket policies.
wrongOptionNotes.D: AWS CodeBuild managed container images that support Docker (privileged mode enabled) have the Docker daemon running; the error specifically relates to authentication credentials.

questions.question: A developer is managing an AWS CloudFormation stack that provisions a production web application. During a stack update, a new AWS::EC2::SecurityGroup resource fails to create because of a naming conflict with an existing security group in the VPC. The stack update rolls back, but the rollback itself fails because the security group is referenced by an Elastic Network Interface created by another application. What is the recommended strategy to resolve this deployment deadlock?

options.text: Manually import the conflicting security group into the CloudFormation stack using resource import.
Delete the failing resource from the CloudFormation template and trigger another update stack command.
Use the AWS CLI or console to perform a CloudFormation continue-update-rollback operation after manually releasing or deleting the blocking dependency.
Delete the entire VPC and all associated stacks to clear out conflicting resources.

questions.explanation: When a CloudFormation stack enters an `UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED` state due to external dependencies preventing resource deletion, the developer must manually resolve the underlying dependency (e.g., disassociating or deleting the conflicting network interface) and then execute `aws cloudformation continue-update-rollback`.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Resource import cannot be performed while a stack is stuck in an UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED state.
wrongOptionNotes.B: CloudFormation does not allow updating a stack while a rollback is actively failing; the rollback state must be resolved first.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Deleting the entire VPC is extremely disruptive and unnecessary for resolving a single stack rollback failure.

questions.question: A developer has set up an AWS CodePipeline pipeline that builds a static React application and deploys it to an Amazon S3 bucket configured for static website hosting. After a successful pipeline run, users visiting the site receive an HTTP 403 Forbidden error for all paths except the root URL. What is the root cause of this deployment issue?

options.text: Amazon S3 static website hosting requires a CloudFront distribution in front of it to resolve 403 errors.
The CodePipeline IAM role lacks s3:PutBucketPolicy permissions to make the bucket publicly readable.
The buildspec file failed to compile the JavaScript bundles, resulting in an empty S3 bucket.

The React application uses client-side routing, and S3 static website hosting attempts to look up physical files for sub-routes, resulting in access denials or missing file errors; the S3 bucket error page must be configured to redirect all requests to index.html.

questions.explanation: Single-page applications (SPAs) built with React rely on client-side routing. When hosted on Amazon S3 static website hosting, requesting a sub-path directly causes S3 to search for a corresponding file. To fix this, the S3 bucket's error document must be configured to return index.html with a 200 status code.

wrongOptionNotes.A: S3 static website hosting works natively without CloudFront, provided bucket policies and error pages are correctly configured.
wrongOptionNotes.B: If the pipeline lacked permissions to upload files or set policies, the deployment phase would have failed completely.
wrongOptionNotes.C: An empty bucket would typically return a 404 Not Found error rather than a 403 Forbidden error.

questions.question: A developer is configuring an AWS CodeDeploy deployment for an application running on an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group. The deployment fails consistently during the ApplicationStop lifecycle event because the deployment script cannot locate the application configuration file. Where does CodeDeploy execute lifecycle event scripts by default on EC2 instances?

options.text: Inside the temporary /tmp/codedeploy/ workspace which is cleared after each lifecycle hook.
Directly from the Amazon S3 bucket where the application revision is stored.
Inside the /var/www/html/ root directory regardless of the application bundle structure.
Inside the /opt/codedeploy-agent/deployment-root/deployment-group-ID/deployment-ID/archived/ directory structure.

questions.explanation: The CodeDeploy agent downloads application revisions to a dedicated local directory structure (typically under `/opt/codedeploy-agent/`) on EC2 instances. Lifecycle scripts execute relative to this extracted bundle location, requiring developers to use relative paths or environment variables defined in appspec.yml.

wrongOptionNotes.A: CodeDeploy maintains deployment artifacts in the persistent agent deployment root directory during the deployment process.
wrongOptionNotes.B: The CodeDeploy agent downloads the revision bundle to the local EC2 instance before executing lifecycle scripts.
wrongOptionNotes.C: CodeDeploy does not assume /var/www/html/ is the target directory unless explicitly specified in the appspec.yml destination parameter.

questions.question: A developer is writing an AWS CloudFormation template that deploys an Amazon DynamoDB table and an AWS Lambda function that reads from the table. To follow security best practices, the developer wants to output the DynamoDB table's Amazon Resource Name (ARN) so other stacks can reference it, but wants to prevent accidental deletion or modification of the table stack. Which CloudFormation feature should the developer implement?

options.text: An IAM service role assigned to CloudFormation with read-only permissions to DynamoDB.
The DeletionPolicy attribute set to Retain on the Lambda function resource.
Enabling Termination Protection on the CloudFormation stack export parameters.
Stack policies configured to Deny Update and Delete actions on the DynamoDB table resource.

questions.explanation: CloudFormation stack policies are JSON documents that define what update actions can be performed on designated resources. By applying a stack policy that denies Update and Delete actions on stateful resources like DynamoDB tables, developers protect production infrastructure from accidental modification.

wrongOptionNotes.A: CloudFormation requires elevated permissions to create and manage resources; restricting CloudFormation itself prevents stack creation.
wrongOptionNotes.B: DeletionPolicy applies to the lifecycle of the resource when the stack is deleted, but does not protect against accidental stack updates or modifications.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Termination protection prevents the entire stack from being deleted, but stack policies offer granular control over specific resource updates and deletions.

questions.question: A developer is configuring an AWS CodeBuild project to build a Java application that requires downloading proprietary Maven dependencies from a secure corporate artifact repository. The corporate repository requires basic authentication credentials stored securely. What is the most secure and effective way to provide these credentials to CodeBuild during the build phase?

options.text: Store the credentials in AWS Secrets Manager or Systems Manager Parameter Store, and reference them as secure environment variables in the CodeBuild project configuration so CodeBuild injects them at runtime.
Include the credentials inside a settings.xml file committed directly to the application source code repository.
Store the username and password as plaintext environment variables directly within the CodeBuild project settings in the AWS Management Console.
Hardcode the credentials inside the buildspec.yml file using echo statements.

questions.explanation: AWS CodeBuild integrates directly with AWS Secrets Manager and AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. Developers can reference secure parameters or secrets in the project configuration, allowing CodeBuild to inject them as environment variables securely during build execution.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Committing credentials to source control repositories introduces severe security risks and leaks secrets.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Storing credentials as plaintext environment variables exposes them in the console and build logs, violating security best practices.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Hardcoding secrets in buildspec files exposes them in build logs and source repositories.

questions.question: An enterprise developer is troubleshooting an AWS CloudFormation deployment failure in a shared services account. A nested stack fails to create because a custom IAM role resource encounters an 'Explicit Deny' error from an active Service Control Policy (SCP) applied at the AWS Organizations root level. How should the developer resolve this deployment blocker?

options.text: Add a statement to the IAM role trusting the CloudFormation execution service principal with full administrator access.
Modify the IAM role resource in the CloudFormation template to inherit administrative privileges from the CloudFormation service-managed role.
Collaborate with the AWS Organization administrator to adjust the SCP boundaries or exclude the target deployment account/OU from the conflicting policy constraints.
Add the aws:PrincipalOrgID condition to the CloudFormation execution role trust policy.

questions.explanation: AWS Organizations Service Control Policies (SCPs) define the maximum available permissions for member accounts. Because an SCP 'Explicit Deny' overrides all IAM policies, infrastructure templates attempting actions prohibited by an SCP will fail until organization-level policies are adjusted.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Trust policies govern who can assume a role, but SCPs filter what actions can be executed within the account, overriding resource-based and identity-based permissions.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Service Control Policies (SCPs) act as guardrails that evaluate against all IAM principals in an account regardless of administrative permissions.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Trust policy conditions do not bypass SCP restrictions enforced by AWS Organizations.

questions.question: A developer is configuring an AWS CodePipeline pipeline that includes an AWS CodeBuild action. The developer notices that subsequent pipeline runs take a long time because dependencies (such as npm packages) are downloaded from the internet every time the build executes. How can the developer optimize the pipeline to cache these dependencies across builds?

options.text: Increase the CodeBuild compute fleet size from BUILD_GENERAL1_SMALL to BUILD_GENERAL1_LARGE.
Enable CodeBuild local caching by selecting local cache modes (such as source, docker layers, or custom) in the CodeBuild project configuration and specifying cache directories in the buildspec.
Configure CodePipeline to keep the build container alive between executions using persistent container settings.
Store the node_modules directory in an Amazon DynamoDB table and write a custom pre-build script to query and restore dependencies.

questions.explanation: AWS CodeBuild provides caching features using Amazon S3 or local caching modes (such as custom or docker layers). Configuring caching for dependency directories (like ~/.npm or node_modules) reduces build duration by avoiding repeated downloads.

wrongOptionNotes.A: While a larger compute type increases CPU and memory, it does not prevent packages from being re-downloaded over the network unless caching is configured.
wrongOptionNotes.C: CodeBuild containers are ephemeral and terminate immediately after a build completes; caching mechanisms must be used to persist files.
wrongOptionNotes.D: DynamoDB is not designed for storing large file archives like node_modules packages.

questions.question: A developer is writing an AWS CloudFormation template that deploys an application consisting of an AWS Lambda function and an Amazon S3 bucket. The developer needs to upload local deployment code stored in a directory on their workstation directly into the Lambda function via CloudFormation. What is the correct approach to reference local code in a CloudFormation template?

options.text: Upload the code manually to an S3 bucket and hardcode the S3 object URL in the CloudFormation template.
Reference the local path in the Code property of the AWS::Lambda::Function resource, and deploy using the AWS CLI package and deploy commands.
Reference the local directory path directly in the S3Bucket and S3Key properties of the Lambda function.
Embed the zipped base64-encoded binary string directly into the CloudFormation template Code property.

questions.explanation: CloudFormation templates cannot natively upload local files to S3 during a standard stack creation unless packaged first. Developers use `aws cloudformation package` to zip local assets, upload them to an Amazon S3 staging bucket, and output a packaged template ready for deployment.

wrongOptionNotes.A: While hardcoding S3 references works, it is a manual process that lacks automated packaging support provided by the AWS CLI.
wrongOptionNotes.C: CloudFormation S3Bucket and S3Key properties require existing S3 bucket names and object keys, not local filesystem paths.
wrongOptionNotes.D: While base64 strings are supported for very small inline scripts, larger deployment packages exceed CloudFormation template size limits and require S3 storage.

questions.question: A developer is configuring an AWS Elastic Beanstalk deployment for a web application. During deployment, the health check fails because the application takes 90 seconds to initialize its database connection pool before responding to HTTP requests on port 80. The default Elastic Beanstalk health check times out after 30 seconds. How should the developer resolve this deployment issue?

options.text: Modify the Elastic Beanstalk environment configuration to increase the health check command timeout and adjust the process manager settings for slow-starting applications.
Attach an Amazon SNS topic to Elastic Beanstalk to suppress health check alerts during the first 5 minutes of deployment.
Downgrade the EC2 instance type to a smaller size so the instance boots faster.
Rewrite the application to perform database connection initialization asynchronously after starting the HTTP server.

questions.explanation: Applications with long startup times can cause Elastic Beanstalk health checks to fail prematurely. Developers can configure target group health check parameters (such as interval, timeout, and healthy threshold) or use application-specific configuration files to adjust startup behavior.

wrongOptionNotes.B: SNS topics notify about events but do not alter how the load balancer or platform evaluates health checks.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Smaller instance types provide less compute capacity and would likely increase application startup and initialization times rather than decrease them.
wrongOptionNotes.D: While asynchronous initialization is an architectural best practice, configuring the platform's health check grace period or timeout is the immediate deployment configuration fix.

questions.question: An application running on Amazon EC2 needs to access objects in an Amazon S3 bucket securely without embedding long-lived credentials in the instance code or configuration files. As a security best practice, how should the developer configure access?

options.text: Configure the Amazon S3 bucket policy to allow unauthenticated public read access specifically for the public IP address of the EC2 instance.
Attach an IAM role to the Amazon EC2 instance profile that grants permissions solely to the required S3 bucket actions.
Attach an inline policy to the default Amazon EC2 service role granting full administrator access to all Amazon S3 buckets.
Store the IAM user access key and secret access key in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store and retrieve them dynamically at runtime.

questions.explanation: AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles for Amazon EC2 allow applications running on instances to securely make API requests to AWS services like Amazon S3 using temporary credentials managed automatically by AWS.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Public S3 bucket policies create severe security vulnerabilities and data leakage risks, making them inappropriate for internal application data.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Granting full administrator access violates the principle of least privilege, exposing the environment to unnecessary security risks.
wrongOptionNotes.D: While Parameter Store secures secrets, using IAM user credentials introduces unnecessary long-lived key management risks compared to native IAM roles.

questions.question: A developer is writing an AWS Lambda function that must invoke another internal Lambda function securely. The function needs to obtain temporary credentials to make SDK calls while ensuring that least-privilege principles are strictly maintained. What is the most secure and idiomatic way to grant permissions?

options.text: Assign an IAM execution role to the Lambda function with permissions scoped specifically to the target Lambda function's ARN.
Embed the AWS account root credentials as environment variables in the Lambda configuration settings.
Attach an execution role to the Lambda function containing a resource-based policy and specific IAM actions for invocation.
Attach an AmazonS3FullAccess policy to the Lambda execution role to ensure there are no permission errors during runtime.

questions.explanation: Every AWS Lambda function has an associated IAM role called the execution role. By scoping the permissions in this role to only the necessary resources and actions, developers adhere to the principle of least privilege.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Embedding root credentials is a severe security violation that exposes the entire AWS account to complete compromise.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Lambda functions use an execution role (an IAM role with a trust policy) rather than attaching resource-based policies to themselves for outgoing calls.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Attaching full access policies violates the principle of least privilege and grants excessive permissions.

questions.question: An enterprise developer needs to ensure that all newly created Amazon S3 buckets across multiple AWS accounts automatically enforce encryption at rest and block public access. Which service configuration should the developer implement to enforce this compliance guardrail organization-wide?

options.text: Apply an AWS Organizations Service Control Policy (SCP) and S3 Account-level Public Access Block along with S3 Centralized Bucket Policies.
Rely on developers to manually check compliance checkboxes in the AWS Management Console during bucket creation.
Deploy AWS CloudTrail to monitor S3 bucket creation and trigger an AWS Lambda function to apply bucket policies retroactively.
Write a shell script that runs nightly via cron on a developer's local machine to scan all S3 buckets and update their settings.

questions.explanation: Preventive guardrails like AWS Organizations Service Control Policies (SCPs) and Amazon S3 account-level Public Access Block settings enforce compliance across accounts by blocking non-compliant requests at the control plane level.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Manual compliance checks are unreliable and fail to enforce mandatory enterprise security guardrails.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Reactive remediation using CloudTrail and Lambda leaves a security window where unencrypted or public buckets exist before the function runs.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Relying on manual scripts run from local machines is insecure, error-prone, and fails to provide continuous organizational compliance.

questions.question: A developer is configuring an Amazon API Gateway REST API integrated with an AWS Lambda backend. The developer needs to secure the endpoint so that only authorized clients possessing a specific cryptographic API key can access it, while also tracking usage quotas. What combination of features should be implemented?

options.text: Attach an open IAM policy to the API Gateway execution role allowing anonymous public access from any IP address.
Configure an API Key, associate it with a Usage Plan, and require the API key on the API method deployment settings.
Embed the API key directly in the client-side JavaScript source code of a public single-page application without restriction.
Rely solely on Amazon CloudWatch alarms to block incoming HTTP traffic when traffic volume exceeds normal thresholds.

questions.explanation: API Gateway supports API keys and usage plans to control access to APIs and enforce throttling and quota limits per client.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Open IAM policies allow unauthenticated public access, which directly contradicts the requirement to secure the endpoint.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Embedding API keys in public client-side code exposes them to extraction and unauthorized usage.
wrongOptionNotes.D: CloudWatch alarms are reactive monitoring tools and cannot authenticate or authorize incoming API requests.

questions.question: An application running on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate requires access to database connection strings and API secrets stored securely in AWS Secrets Manager. What is the most secure method to inject these secrets into the container runtime environment?

options.text: Hardcode the secret values directly into the plaintext container definition environment variables within the ECS task definition.
Reference the Secrets Manager secret ARN in the ECS task definition container definition secrets section, allowing ECS to inject them securely at startup.
Store the secrets in a public GitHub repository and configure the container to clone the repository upon startup.
Write the secrets to an unencrypted text file stored on the ephemeral root storage of the Fargate task container.

questions.explanation: ECS task definitions support referencing Secrets Manager secrets directly. ECS retrieves the secret value securely at task launch and injects it into the container environment or mounts it as a file.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Hardcoding secrets in task definition environment variables exposes them in plaintext to anyone with read access to the ECS configuration.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Storing secrets in a public repository compromises them immediately and completely violates security standards.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Unencrypted text files on ephemeral storage can be accessed if the container is compromised or inspected.

questions.question: A developer needs to ensure that an AWS CodeBuild project compiling proprietary source code does not leak sensitive environment variables or AWS credentials in its build logs. Which security practice should be implemented?

options.text: Store sensitive build secrets in AWS Secrets Manager or Systems Manager Parameter Store, and reference them securely in the buildspec file.
Disable AWS CloudTrail logging for the CodeBuild project to prevent log files from being generated.
Define all database passwords and API tokens as plaintext environment variables in the CodeBuild project configuration settings.
Print all environment variables to standard output at the beginning of every build step for debugging purposes.

questions.explanation: AWS CodeBuild allows referencing secrets from Systems Manager Parameter Store or Secrets Manager in the buildspec file, preventing sensitive data from being logged or exposed in plaintext environment configurations.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Disabling logging violates audit and compliance requirements without solving the core secret exposure issue.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Plaintext environment variables in build configurations can be viewed by anyone with DescribeBuilds permissions and may appear in logs.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Printing environment variables to standard output dumps secrets directly into the build logs.

questions.question: An Amazon DynamoDB table stores customer profile data containing personally identifiable information (PII). Compliance requirements mandate that all data must be encrypted at rest using a customer-managed key with strict key rotation policies. How should the developer configure this?

options.text: Configure the DynamoDB table encryption settings to use an AWS KMS customer managed key (CMK).
Use the default AWS owned key provided by DynamoDB since it automatically complies with all enterprise regulations.
Write a custom application-layer encryption routine using a hardcoded AES key before writing items to DynamoDB.
Disable encryption entirely and rely on Amazon VPC security groups to protect access to the table.

questions.explanation: Amazon DynamoDB supports encryption at rest using AWS KMS customer managed keys (CMKs), enabling organizations to meet compliance mandates for data protection and key lifecycle management.

wrongOptionNotes.B: AWS owned keys do not give the organization control over key rotation schedules or access policies required for strict compliance.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Hardcoding encryption keys in application code introduces significant security risks and key management overhead.
wrongOptionNotes.D: DynamoDB is a public endpoint service accessed via HTTPS; VPC security groups do not provide encryption at rest for stored data.

questions.question: An AWS Lambda function needs to assume an IAM role in another trusted AWS account to access a cross-account Amazon S3 bucket. What configuration steps are required to establish this securely?

options.text: Hardcode the target account's root access keys directly into the Lambda function's source code.
Share the AWS account root user password with the developer administering the secondary account.
Attach an AdministratorAccess policy to the Lambda function without configuring any trust policies.

Configure the Lambda execution role with a trust policy allowing it to be assumed, and configure a cross-account IAM role in the target account with a resource policy trusting the Lambda execution role.

questions.explanation: Cross-account access in AWS requires configuring IAM roles with appropriate trust policies that explicitly permit the calling principal to assume the role using AWS STS AssumeRole.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Hardcoding long-lived access keys creates extreme security vulnerabilities.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Sharing root passwords violates fundamental security and access management policies.
wrongOptionNotes.C: AdministratorAccess without trust policies does not grant cross-account permissions and violates least privilege.

questions.question: A developer is building a serverless application using AWS SAM. The application includes an Amazon API Gateway and an AWS Lambda function. The security team mandates that all API requests must be authenticated using JSON Web Tokens (JWT) issued by an OpenID Connect (OIDC) compliant identity provider. How should the developer configure this in the SAM template?

options.text: Disable authentication on API Gateway and implement manual JWT parsing and signature verification inside every Lambda function handler.
Use basic HTTP authentication with static usernames and passwords stored in plaintext environment variables.
Configure an API Gateway Lambda authorizer or HTTP API JWT authorizer referencing the OIDC provider issuer URL and audience.
Rely on AWS IAM authentication for all public internet users visiting the single-page application.

questions.explanation: Amazon API Gateway supports JWT authorizers for HTTP APIs, allowing offloading of token validation and signature verification directly to the API Gateway edge before requests reach backend services.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Implementing custom token verification in every Lambda function duplicates code and increases the risk of cryptographic implementation flaws.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Basic authentication with static plaintext credentials fails modern security standards and compliance requirements.
wrongOptionNotes.D: IAM authentication is not suitable for unauthenticated public internet users or external OIDC identity federation.

questions.question: A developer is managing an Amazon S3 bucket that contains sensitive financial reports. A security audit reveals that unauthorized users within the same AWS account have been accessing the bucket. What is the most effective policy mechanism to explicitly deny access to unauthorized users regardless of their IAM permissions?

options.text: Rely exclusively on IAM user policies without configuring any S3 bucket policies.
Delete all IAM policies attached to the unauthorized users and remove them from the AWS account entirely.
Apply an explicit Deny statement in the S3 bucket policy targeting the unauthorized IAM users or roles.
Enable Amazon S3 Versioning to track changes made by unauthorized users.

questions.explanation: In AWS IAM evaluation logic, an explicit Deny statement always overrides any Allow statements. Applying an explicit Deny in an S3 bucket policy is a definitive way to restrict resource access.

wrongOptionNotes.A: IAM user policies alone can be circumvented if other roles or cross-account policies grant broad access to the bucket.
wrongOptionNotes.B: While removing users works if they are no longer needed, bucket policies provide granular resource-level control when users require access to other services.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Versioning protects against accidental overwrites and deletions, but does not prevent unauthorized data access.

questions.question: An application running on Amazon EC2 instances needs to securely sign requests to AWS services. The security team mandates that IAM roles used by the instances must enforce a session duration limit of no more than 1 hour. How can this be configured?

options.text: Rely on default AWS settings since IAM role sessions automatically expire after exactly 1 minute.
Write a custom cron job that deletes the instance metadata service every hour.
Configure the maximum session duration property on the IAM role when creating or modifying the role.
Modify the operating system kernel configuration on each Amazon EC2 instance to terminate authentication tokens every 60 minutes.

questions.explanation: AWS IAM roles support setting a maximum session duration parameter, allowing security administrators to control how long temporary security credentials remain valid before requiring refresh.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Default IAM role session durations for EC2 instances typically last 1 hour or more depending on configuration, and default to 1 hour when assumed via STS.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Deleting instance metadata services disrupts instance operations and does not control IAM token validity periods.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Instance operating system configurations do not control AWS IAM session token durations.

questions.question: A developer is writing an AWS Lambda function that connects to an Amazon RDS PostgreSQL database inside a private VPC subnet. To adhere to strict security hardening guidelines, how should database credentials be handled and retrieved?

options.text: Store the database credentials in a public text file in an Amazon S3 bucket with public read permissions.
Store the database username and password in plaintext within the Lambda function environment variables.
Embed the superuser database credentials directly in the Python source code file.
Retrieve database credentials securely at runtime from AWS Secrets Manager using IAM permissions granted to the Lambda execution role.

questions.explanation: AWS Secrets Manager provides secure storage and automated rotation for database credentials, which can be retrieved securely by Lambda execution roles at runtime.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Public S3 text files expose sensitive database credentials to the entire internet.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Plaintext environment variables can be viewed by anyone with read access to the Lambda configuration.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Hardcoding credentials in source code creates severe security risks and complicates secret rotation.

questions.question: An organization wants to prevent developers from accidentally creating Amazon S3 buckets with public read or write access across all development AWS accounts. Which AWS feature should the security administrator configure to enforce this globally?

options.text: Configuring individual IAM user policies for every developer to check a compliance box.
Disabling Amazon S3 access entirely across all AWS accounts.
Sending daily email notifications to developers reminding them not to make buckets public.
AWS Organizations Service Control Policies (SCPs) denying the s3:PutBucketPublicAccessBlock deletion or weakening actions.

questions.explanation: AWS Organizations Service Control Policies (SCPs) establish guardrails that centrally control permissions across multiple AWS accounts, preventing users from bypassing security baselines.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Manual compliance checking is inefficient and prone to human error.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Disabling S3 entirely would break all applications requiring object storage.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Email reminders are reactive and do not technically prevent non-compliant resource creation.

questions.question: A developer has deployed a web application on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The application processes sensitive customer payment records. Security compliance dictates that all data in transit must be encrypted using strong TLS ciphers. How should the developer configure the Application Load Balancer?

options.text: Terminate TLS at the EC2 instances while keeping the ALB listener configured for plain HTTP traffic.
Disable all SSL certificates to allow custom self-signed cryptographic bypasses.
Configure an HTTPS listener on the ALB using an ACM-managed certificate and a secure predefined security policy for SSL negotiation.
Configure an HTTP listener on port 80 and rely on client browsers to encrypt traffic automatically.

questions.explanation: Application Load Balancers support HTTPS listeners with AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) SSL/TLS certificates and predefined security policies that enforce robust cipher suites for data in transit.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Terminating TLS on EC2 without ALB-level encryption leaves traffic between the client and ALB unencrypted.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Self-signed certificates without proper validation compromise end-to-end security and trust.
wrongOptionNotes.D: HTTP traffic is unencrypted plaintext and fails all data-in-transit security and compliance requirements.

questions.question: A developer needs to share an encrypted Amazon S3 object with an external partner in a separate AWS account. The object is encrypted using a customer-managed AWS KMS key. What must the developer configure to allow the external partner to decrypt the object?

options.text: Update the KMS key policy to grant decrypt permissions to the external AWS account's IAM principal, and grant cross-account read access on the S3 object.
Disable encryption on the S3 object before sharing it with the external partner.
Send the KMS key ARN and plaintext master key via unencrypted email to the external partner.
Make the S3 bucket completely public so any external user can download and decrypt the object without authentication.

questions.explanation: When sharing KMS-encrypted S3 objects cross-account, authorization must be granted on both the S3 bucket/object level and the AWS KMS customer managed key policy.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Disabling encryption violates compliance mandates protecting sensitive data.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Sending keys via email compromises cryptographic material and violates all security best practices.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Making the bucket public violates data security standards and does not solve KMS decryption authorization for encrypted objects.

questions.question: A developer manages a high-throughput data processing pipeline where an AWS Lambda function polls an Amazon SQS standard queue and invokes downstream third-party APIs. During peak hours, the downstream APIs struggle with request volume, resulting in throttling errors. The developer must reduce unnecessary Lambda invocations and lower overall costs without dropping incoming messages.

options.text: Switch the queue from a standard SQS queue to an SQS FIFO queue to enforce sequential processing.
Add a Redis cache layer in front of the SQS queue to deduplicate messages before they reach Lambda.
Configure Amazon SQS batching by setting the batch size on the event source mapping to a higher value up to 10.
Increase the Lambda function timeout and memory allocation to handle API retries more efficiently.

questions.explanation: Configuring event source mapping batch sizes allows AWS Lambda to process up to 10 messages per invocation for SQS queues. This directly decreases the total number of Lambda invocations, reducing both AWS compute costs and the pressure on downstream APIs.

wrongOptionNotes.A: FIFO queues restrict throughput and do not reduce the number of Lambda invocations required to process the message volume.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Caching standard SQS messages does not inherently reduce Lambda invocations unless messages are strictly duplicates, and provisioning Redis adds unnecessary infrastructure overhead and cost.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Increasing timeout and memory does not reduce invocation counts or address downstream throttling; it only increases operational costs.

questions.question: An analytics application running on Amazon EC2 instances processes large volumes of data files stored in Amazon S3. The application currently downloads entire files over the public internet, resulting in high NAT Gateway and data transfer expenses. The developer needs to minimize network costs while ensuring high-speed data retrieval.

options.text: Create an Amazon S3 Gateway VPC Endpoint in the VPC and route S3 traffic through it.
Provision an NAT instance instead of an NAT Gateway to reduce hourly infrastructure fees.
Migrate the EC2 instances to a different Availability Zone to take advantage of lower inter-AZ pricing.
Enable Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket to optimize data download speeds.

questions.explanation: Gateway VPC endpoints for Amazon S3 allow resources within a VPC to communicate with S3 without traversing the internet or passing through NAT Gateways, completely eliminating NAT data processing fees at zero additional hourly charge.

wrongOptionNotes.B: NAT instances still route traffic over the internet and do not eliminate data processing charges for S3 traffic, plus they introduce single points of failure.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Accessing S3 from EC2 does not incur inter-AZ charges, and changing zones does not resolve NAT Gateway data processing fees.
wrongOptionNotes.D: S3 Transfer Acceleration optimizes uploads using AWS Edge Locations, but it incurs additional per-gigabyte fees and does not reduce VPC-to-S3 networking costs.

questions.question: A financial reporting service uses an Amazon DynamoDB table with On-Demand capacity mode. As business has grown, the monthly AWS bill has spiked unexpectedly due to read and write request units. The workload exhibits a predictable, steady daily pattern with low traffic at night and high traffic during business hours. The developer needs to optimize costs without risking throttling.

options.text: Compress all item attributes in application code before writing them to the DynamoDB table.
Switch the DynamoDB table capacity mode from On-Demand to Provisioned with auto scaling enabled.
Implement Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) in front of the table to cache read requests.
Partition the DynamoDB table into multiple smaller tables to distribute the request load.

questions.explanation: For predictable or steady-state workloads, Provisioned capacity mode with Auto Scaling enabled is substantially cheaper than On-Demand mode because On-Demand pricing carries an inherent premium for flexibility.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Compression reduces storage size, but DynamoDB billing is based on Read/Write Request Units (RCUs/WCUs), not storage capacity alone.
wrongOptionNotes.C: While DAX reduces read units for read-heavy workloads, running a persistent cluster incurs constant hourly node costs which may exceed savings if the baseline write volume is also high.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Partitioning manually adds application complexity and does not change the fundamental pricing structure of On-Demand request units.

questions.question: An enterprise web application runs on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate. The application experiences steady traffic during business hours and minimal traffic overnight. The developer needs to optimize the compute spend for the ECS service while maintaining high availability.

options.text: Configure Amazon ECS Service Auto Scaling with target tracking scaling policies based on CPU utilization.
Reduce the CPU and memory allocation in the task definition to the lowest possible tier.
Set the desired task count to zero every evening using a custom AWS Lambda cron script.
Migrate the ECS tasks from AWS Fargate to the EC2 launch type using reserved instances.

questions.explanation: ECS Service Auto Scaling dynamically adjusts the number of tasks running in your service based on CloudWatch metrics, ensuring you only pay for the Fargate compute resources needed at any given time.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Lowering task resources arbitrarily will cause application instability and errors during peak business hours.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Setting desired tasks to zero completely drops availability overnight, which violates the high availability requirement.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Reserved instances require steady 24/7 utilization to be cost-effective; fluctuating overnight traffic would leave EC2 capacity underutilized.

questions.question: A developer is optimizing an AWS Lambda function that executes every 5 minutes to aggregate telemetry logs. The function currently runs for 3 seconds with a memory configuration of 2048 MB. Analysis reveals that the function's CPU usage is low and it is not memory-bound. The developer wants to minimize execution costs.

options.text: Migrate the Lambda function logic to an Amazon ECS task running on Fargate Spot.
Increase the memory allocation to 10248 MB to leverage multiple vCPUs and finish faster.
Configure provisioned concurrency for the Lambda function to eliminate cold starts.
Decrease the memory allocation to 512 MB and test the execution duration.

questions.explanation: AWS Lambda allocates CPU power linearly proportional to the memory configured. If a function does not benefit from additional CPU or memory, reducing the memory setting reduces the cost per millisecond of execution.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Running a short-lived 3-second task every 5 minutes on ECS introduces unnecessary infrastructure overhead, startup latency, and higher baseline costs compared to Lambda.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Increasing memory increases the cost per millisecond proportionally. If a function is not CPU-bound, higher memory does not yield a proportional speedup, resulting in higher net costs.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Provisioned concurrency incurs continuous hourly charges, which dramatically increases the cost for a function invoked infrequently every 5 minutes.

questions.question: A media streaming platform stores user-uploaded thumbnails in an Amazon S3 bucket. Millions of thumbnails are generated daily, but 90% of them are rarely accessed after 30 days, while the remaining 10% are accessed frequently. The storage costs for the S3 bucket are growing rapidly. What is the most cost-effective way to optimize storage?

options.text: Move all objects manually to Amazon EBS volumes attached to an EC2 instance.
Create an S3 Lifecycle policy to transition all objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 30 days.
Delete all objects older than 30 days using an S3 Lifecycle expiration rule.
Enable Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering on the S3 bucket.

questions.explanation: Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering is designed for data with unknown or changing access patterns. It automatically optimizes storage costs by moving objects between access tiers when access patterns change, with no retrieval fees.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Storing millions of files on EBS is significantly more expensive and complex than using native S3 storage classes.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Transitioning all objects to Glacier Deep Archive would make the 10% frequently accessed thumbnails subject to retrieval fees and long retrieval times.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Deleting objects permanently removes user data, violating business requirements since some thumbnails are still accessed.

questions.question: An application hosted on Amazon EC2 downloads large reference datasets from an Amazon S3 bucket within the same AWS Region. The network monitoring tool shows excessive data transfer fees associated with traffic leaving the VPC. How can the developer resolve this issue cost-effectively?

options.text: Configure a VPC peering connection between the EC2 VPC and the S3 service VPC.
Create an Amazon S3 Gateway VPC Endpoint and ensure the VPC route tables point to it.
Attach an Elastic IP address directly to every EC2 instance downloading the data.
Replace the default route table configuration with a custom NAT Gateway route.

questions.explanation: Gateway VPC Endpoints for Amazon S3 enable private, secure connectivity to S3 from within a VPC without incurring data transfer or NAT processing fees.

wrongOptionNotes.A: AWS services like S3 do not support VPC peering connections; VPC endpoints must be used instead.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Elastic IPs route traffic over the public internet and do not eliminate data transfer fees for accessing S3.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Routing traffic through a NAT Gateway for intra-region AWS traffic incurs both data processing and transfer charges.

questions.question: A developer has deployed a serverless API using Amazon API Gateway and AWS Lambda. During off-peak hours, low traffic causes sporadic requests, but users complain of high latency on the first request due to cold starts. The business requires low latency 24/7 but wants to minimize the financial impact.

options.text: Increase the memory allocation of the Lambda function to 10248 MB permanently.
Migrate the API backend from AWS Lambda to always-running Amazon EC2 Reserved Instances.
Set up an Amazon EventBridge rule to invoke the Lambda function every minute to keep it warm.
Configure Provisioned Concurrency for the Lambda function targeting the expected off-peak concurrency level.

questions.explanation: Provisioned Concurrency initializes a requested number of execution environments so they are ready to respond immediately, solving cold-start latency while allowing precise cost management.

wrongOptionNotes.A: While higher memory slightly reduces initialization time, it does not eliminate cold starts entirely and greatly increases compute costs for all invocations.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Running EC2 instances 24/7 for low off-peak traffic is far more expensive and less elastic than serverless architectures.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Invoking a function every minute generates unnecessary invocation charges and does not prevent concurrent cold starts if multiple users arrive simultaneously.

questions.question: An image processing pipeline runs on an Amazon EKS cluster deployed across multiple Availability Zones. The pods pull raw images from Amazon S3 and push processed images back. Due to high data volume, the inter-AZ data transfer costs are excessively high. The developer needs to redesign the deployment to reduce network costs.

options.text: Deploy a local caching proxy within each Availability Zone to cache processed images.
Optimize the EKS cluster topology so that data-intensive pods and their corresponding dependencies run within a single Availability Zone where applicable, or use local caching.
Configure Kubernetes node affinity to schedule pods in the same Availability Zone where the S3 gateway endpoint traffic is localized.
Use NAT Gateways in each Availability Zone to route S3 traffic securely.

questions.explanation: Cross-AZ data transfer charges in Kubernetes clusters often accumulate when pods communicate across zones. Optimizing pod scheduling and utilizing topology-aware routing reduces unnecessary inter-AZ traffic.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Caching processed images does not address raw image retrieval or inter-AZ communication overhead between cluster nodes and storage.
wrongOptionNotes.C: S3 Gateway VPC endpoints are regional constructs, and S3 requests do not incur inter-AZ data transfer charges regardless of the AZ from which they originate.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Routing S3 traffic through NAT Gateways introduces heavy data processing charges per gigabyte, increasing costs significantly.

questions.question: A company runs a batch processing job on Amazon EC2 Spot Instances managed by an Auto Scaling group. Occasionally, Spot Instances are interrupted, causing job failures and requiring manual restarts. The developer needs to ensure high fault tolerance and cost efficiency for short-lived batch jobs.

options.text: Purchase Standard Reserved Instances for the entire maximum potential batch capacity.
Configure the Auto Scaling group to use multiple instance types across multiple Availability Zones and enable AWS Fault Injection Simulator.
Design the batch application to be stateless, use checkpointing, and configure the Auto Scaling group with a diversified pool of Spot instance types.
Replace all Spot Instances with On-Demand Instances to guarantee uninterrupted execution.

questions.explanation: Spot Instances provide massive cost savings but can be interrupted with a 2-minute warning. Designing applications to be stateless and checkpoint progress, combined with diversified instance pools, ensures resilience and maximum cost efficiency.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Purchasing reserved instances for sporadic batch jobs results in wasted capacity and higher idle costs.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Fault Injection Simulator is for chaos engineering experiments, not for handling Spot instance interruption mitigation.
wrongOptionNotes.D: While On-Demand instances prevent interruptions, they eliminate the cost savings of Spot instances, which offer up to 90% discounts.

questions.question: A developer has built a microservices architecture where services communicate via Amazon SNS and Amazon SQS. During testing, it is discovered that unnecessary messages are being broadcast to multiple queues, resulting in high SQS API request charges and unnecessary Lambda invocations. How can the developer optimize this architecture for cost?

options.text: Increase the polling timeout (ReceiveMessageWaitTimeSeconds) on all SQS queues.
Implement SNS message filtering policies so that subscribers only receive relevant messages.
Batch multiple SNS topics into a single topic to reduce topic management overhead.
Migrate the SNS/SQS architecture to an Amazon EventBridge event bus with custom rules.

questions.explanation: Amazon SNS message filtering allows subscribers to define filter policies. This ensures that SQS queues only receive messages matching specific criteria, eliminating wasted storage, API requests, and downstream processing costs.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Long polling reduces empty receives and API costs for polling, but it does not prevent unwanted messages from being delivered to the queue in the first place.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Consolidating topics does not reduce message duplication or filtering overhead; it increases coupling between microservices.
wrongOptionNotes.D: While EventBridge is powerful, completely rewriting the messaging layer is an architectural overhaul when SNS message filtering natively solves the delivery cost problem.

questions.question: An organization runs an enterprise web application on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The finance department notes that data transfer expenses from the load balancer to the backend instances are extremely high because the instances are spread across multiple AWS Regions. The developer is tasked with optimizing the architecture.

options.text: Deploy an Application Load Balancer and target instances locally within each region, utilizing AWS Global Accelerator to route users to the optimal regional endpoint.
Enable cross-load-balancer routing on the Application Load Balancer.
Replace the Application Load Balancer with Network Load Balancers in every region.
Consolidate all backend EC2 instances into a single AWS Region where the Application Load Balancer resides.

questions.explanation: AWS Global Accelerator improves availability and performance by routing user traffic through AWS's global network infrastructure to regional endpoints, avoiding public internet congestion and reducing data transfer costs.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Cross-load-balancer routing distributes traffic evenly across all registered targets across multiple Availability Zones *within the same region*, not across multiple regions.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Replacing ALB with NLB does not solve multi-region routing or cross-region traffic distribution issues.
wrongOptionNotes.D: An Application Load Balancer cannot route traffic across multiple AWS Regions; ALBs are regional constructs.

questions.question: A development team is storing large log archives in an Amazon S3 bucket. Compliance mandates that logs be retained for 7 years. However, logs older than 90 days are accessed less than once a year. The current S3 Standard storage costs are unsustainable. What is the most cost-effective S3 lifecycle strategy?

options.text: Keep all logs in S3 Standard and enable S3 Intelligent-Tiering from day one.
Delete all log files immediately after 90 days to eliminate storage fees entirely.
Transition objects to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) after 30 days and to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 90 days.
Store the logs directly on Amazon EBS volumes attached to an archiving EC2 instance.

questions.explanation: Using an S3 Lifecycle policy to transition objects from S3 Standard to Infrequent Access tiers and subsequently to archive classes like S3 Glacier provides the lowest possible cost for long-term compliance retention.

wrongOptionNotes.A: While Intelligent-Tiering helps with unknown patterns, S3 Glacier and Glacier Deep Archive offer significantly lower per-gigabyte storage rates for multi-year archive data than Intelligent-Tiering's archive tiers.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Deleting logs violates the 7-year compliance mandate.
wrongOptionNotes.D: EBS storage is substantially more expensive than S3 and Glacier for long-term archival storage.

questions.question: An analytics job runs daily on an Amazon EMR cluster. The job is fault-tolerant, can be interrupted without data loss, and takes approximately 4 hours to complete. The developer needs to optimize the cluster configuration to minimize compute costs.

options.text: Provision the entire EMR cluster using On-Demand Instances with 3-year All Upfront savings plans.
Execute the EMR job inside a single AWS Lambda function with maximum memory allocation.
Configure the core nodes and task nodes to use Spot Instances while keeping the primary node on On-Demand or Reserved Instances.
Configure all EMR nodes, including the primary node, to use Spot Instances.

questions.explanation: EMR cluster cost optimization relies on maintaining a stable primary node using On-Demand or Reserved instances while leveraging Spot instances for core and task nodes where data processing occurs and interruptions can be handled.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Savings plans lock you into long-term commitments, which are inefficient if workloads or data processing frameworks change.
wrongOptionNotes.B: AWS Lambda has a maximum execution timeout of 15 minutes, making it impossible to run a 4-hour EMR analytics job.
wrongOptionNotes.D: The primary (master) node in an EMR cluster must never use Spot instances because its termination causes cluster failure and loss of job coordination.

questions.question: A developer is configuring a high-volume notification service using Amazon SNS and AWS Lambda. Millions of push notifications are sent daily. Many notifications fail due to temporary network issues with endpoint providers, triggering automatic SNS retries that increase costs and execution times. The developer wants to optimize retry handling and reduce unnecessary invocations.

options.text: Implement custom exponential backoff and jitter logic within the Lambda function code for downstream API calls, and adjust the SNS subscription retry policy.
Configure an Amazon SQS dead-letter queue (DLQ) on the Lambda event source mapping to capture failed messages immediately.
Increase the Lambda function timeout to 15 minutes to allow synchronous retries to complete.
Migrate the notification service from SNS to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams.

questions.explanation: Configuring robust delivery retry policies on Amazon SNS combined with intelligent backoff logic in downstream processors prevents cascading failures and eliminates wasted compute charges caused by aggressive retries.

wrongOptionNotes.B: A DLQ captures messages after all retries are exhausted; it does not prevent the retries themselves or reduce initial invocation volume.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Extending timeouts for failing network calls wastes compute resources and increases billing without resolving the underlying connectivity issue.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Kinesis is designed for real-time streaming data ingestion and does not natively solve push notification retry logic or endpoint failure handling.

questions.question: An enterprise web application deployed on Amazon EC2 instances spans both us-east-1 and us-west-2, fronted by Amazon Route 53 using a latency-based routing policy with health checks enabled. During a regional power outage in us-east-1, the EC2 instances in that region become unreachable, but Route 53 continues to route a significant portion of traffic to us-east-1, causing widespread HTTP 5xx errors for end users. What is the most likely cause of this behavior, and how should it be resolved?

options.text: Application Load Balancers cannot be used as targets for Route 53 health checks when spanning multiple regions, requiring direct EC2 public IP health checks.

The Route 53 health check interval and failure threshold are too high, or the unhealthy evaluation interval is misconfigured, causing a delay in detecting the outage. Lowering the evaluation threshold and interval will resolve the issue.
Latency-based routing relies solely on client geographic latency and ignores health check statuses. The routing policy must be changed to failover routing to respect health checks.
Amazon EC2 instances across regions cannot share the same Route 53 record set when using latency routing, leading to split-brain routing behavior.

questions.explanation: Route 53 latency-based routing supports health checks, but failover timing is dictated by the health check configuration (interval, failure threshold). Tuning these parameters ensures rapid detection and redirection of traffic during regional failures.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Route 53 can easily perform health checks directly on Application Load Balancers across multiple AWS regions.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Route 53 latency routing fully supports health checks. When a health check fails, Route 53 automatically removes the unhealthy record from consideration.
